stem: A newly created AWS account will be handed to a product team. Before it is used, a security review requires the root user to be locked down. Which actions should be taken? (Choose TWO.)
options: Enable multi-factor authentication on the root user
Attach a permissions boundary to the root user restricting it to billing
Delete any access keys belonging to the root user and use IAM identities for day-to-day work
Move the root user into an IAM group with limited permissions
Rotate the root access keys every 90 days and store them in Secrets Manager
explanation: The root user cannot be restricted by IAM policies, so the defence is to protect it (MFA) and remove standing credentials (no access keys), using it only for the handful of tasks that require it.
distractors: IAM policies, including permissions boundaries, do not apply to the root user.
The root user is not an IAM user and cannot be placed in a group.
Root access keys should not exist at all; rotating them keeps an unnecessary long-lived credential alive.

stem: An engineer accidentally applied a bucket policy that denies all principals every S3 action on the bucket, and now no IAM administrator can view or delete the policy. How can access be restored?
options: Sign in as the account root user and delete the bucket policy
Attach AdministratorAccess to a new IAM user and delete the policy
Open an AWS Support case; only AWS can remove a bucket policy
Wait for the policy to expire; deny statements are temporary
explanation: An explicit Deny for all principals in the bucket policy blocks every IAM identity. Removing an unusable bucket policy is one of the specific tasks reserved for the account root user.
distractors: The explicit Deny in the bucket policy applies to every IAM principal, including a brand-new administrator.
The root user can fix this without AWS Support involvement.
Policies do not expire; the deny stays until it is removed.

stem: A security team wants a continuous list of every S3 bucket, IAM role, KMS key and SQS queue that is accessible from outside their AWS Organization, and to be told when a new one appears. Which service should they enable?
options: IAM credential report
IAM Access Analyzer
IAM Access Advisor
AWS Trusted Advisor
explanation: IAM Access Analyzer evaluates resource-based policies and reports resources shared with principals outside the account or Organization, generating findings as new external access is granted.
distractors: The credential report is an account-wide CSV about IAM users' passwords and keys, not about resource sharing.
Access Advisor shows which services an identity has actually used, to help trim its permissions; it does not analyse resource policies.
Trusted Advisor has a few S3 permission checks, but it is not a continuous analysis of resource policies across services and Organization boundaries.

stem: A team needs about twenty small development servers that sit almost idle most of the day, with occasional short bursts when tests run. Which instance family is the MOST cost-effective fit?
options: c family instances, which are compute optimised
r family instances, which are memory optimised
t family instances, which are burstable
i family instances, which are storage optimised
explanation: Burstable t instances earn CPU credits while idle and spend them during bursts, so a low, spiky baseline is exactly their design point at the lowest hourly price.
distractors: Compute-optimised instances suit sustained CPU-heavy work like batch and encoding; they are oversized and pricier for idle dev boxes.
Memory-optimised instances target caches and large databases, not idle development servers.
Storage-optimised instances come with local NVMe for very high IOPS; nothing here needs that.

stem: A company runs a fleet of m5.large instances 24/7 for a mature application and is certain the instance type and Region will not change for the next three years. Which purchasing option gives the LARGEST discount?
options: Three-year Standard Reserved Instances for m5.large in that Region
A three-year Compute Savings Plan sized to the fleet's hourly spend
Three-year Convertible Reserved Instances for m5.large in that Region
Spot Instances with a mixed instances policy across several families
explanation: Standard RIs give the deepest discount when the configuration is fixed, and can be resold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace if plans change. The question stresses an unchanging type, which is the RI cue.
distractors: A Compute Savings Plan buys flexibility across families, Regions and Fargate/Lambda at a somewhat smaller discount; flexibility is not needed here.
Convertible RIs allow exchanging for another family at the cost of a smaller discount; the workload does not need that.
Spot can be interrupted with two minutes' notice and is unsuitable for a fleet that must run continuously.

stem: A financial application must always be able to launch a fixed number of a specific instance type in a specific Availability Zone, even during Regional capacity shortages, and the company also wants a discount for the steady usage. Which option provides BOTH?
options: A Compute Savings Plan covering the instances' hourly spend
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the instance family in the Region
Zonal Reserved Instances for the instance type in that AZ
Regional Reserved Instances for the instance type in that Region
explanation: A zonal RI reserves capacity in the named AZ as well as providing the billing discount. Savings Plans and Regional RIs are billing constructs only and do not reserve capacity.
distractors: Savings Plans are purely a pricing commitment; they never reserve capacity.
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan locks a family and Region for a discount but still provides no capacity reservation.
Regional RIs float across AZs for the discount but do not reserve capacity in a specific AZ.

stem: A rendering farm on Spot Instances loses large numbers of nodes at once and jobs stall. The team wants to keep the Spot discount while reducing how often work is interrupted. Which changes help MOST? (Choose TWO.)
options: Request capacity across many instance types and Availability Zones using EC2 Fleet or Spot Fleet
Use the capacity-optimized allocation strategy instead of lowest-price
Request a Spot block for a guaranteed six-hour uninterrupted window
Move all nodes to a single instance type in a cluster placement group
Set the Spot maximum price to ten times the On-Demand price
explanation: Spot is made reliable by diversity: spreading requests across many pools means one pool being reclaimed does not empty the fleet, and capacity-optimized picks the pools with the most spare capacity, which are least likely to be interrupted.
distractors: Spot blocks (defined-duration Spot) are no longer available; a guaranteed uninterrupted window is not something Spot offers.
Concentrating on one type in one placement group is the opposite of diversification and increases the chance everything is reclaimed together.
Interruptions happen when AWS needs the capacity back, not because of your price; overpaying does not prevent reclamation.

stem: A company runs five instances that each host a critical, non-replicated component. A single hardware failure must never take down more than one of them, and they may be spread across Availability Zones. Which placement group type is appropriate?
options: Cluster placement group
No placement group; instead put all five in one dedicated host
Partition placement group
Spread placement group
explanation: A spread placement group places each instance on distinct underlying hardware and can span AZs, giving maximum isolation for a small number of critical instances (up to seven per AZ).
distractors: Cluster packs instances into one rack for low latency, which is exactly the shared failure domain the requirement forbids.
A single dedicated host is one physical server, so a hardware failure would take down all five.
Partition groups separate groups of instances onto different racks; they suit large rack-aware distributed systems rather than isolating individual instances.

stem: An analytics application takes 20 minutes to load a large in-memory dataset after every boot. It is used only during business hours and the team wants to stop paying for compute overnight without the long warm-up each morning. What should they do?
options: Stop the instance each evening and start it again each morning with a scheduled action
Terminate the instance each evening and launch a new one from an AMI each morning
Hibernate the instance each evening so its memory is preserved and restored on start
Leave the instance running and change it to a smaller instance type overnight
explanation: Hibernate writes RAM contents to the encrypted EBS root volume and restores them on start, so the application resumes with its dataset in memory while compute charges stop; the root volume must be encrypted and large enough to hold RAM.
distractors: A stopped instance loses its RAM, so the 20-minute load happens again every morning.
Terminating loses both RAM and the root volume by default; the warm-up would repeat.
Resizing requires a stop, which loses RAM, and continuing to run overnight still incurs compute cost.

stem: An operations team must apply the same configuration command to 500 EC2 instances across several Auto Scaling groups without opening SSH and without logging in to each instance. What should they use?
options: EC2 Instance Connect with a script that loops over every instance ID
AWS Systems Manager Run Command targeting the instances by tag
A bastion host with a shared key pair used to reach every instance
User data on the launch template, applied by rebooting every instance
explanation: SSM Run Command executes a command across a fleet selected by tags or resource groups through the SSM agent, with no inbound ports and no per-instance sessions.
distractors: Instance Connect pushes ephemeral SSH keys to individual public instances; it still requires port 22 and one connection per instance.
A bastion reintroduces open SSH and shared long-lived keys, the pattern modern answers avoid.
User data runs only at first boot, not on reboot, and rebooting a fleet to run one command is disruptive.

stem: A regulatory requirement states that a company's instances must not share physical hardware with other AWS customers. There is no bring-your-own-licence requirement and no need to see or control physical sockets. Which option satisfies the requirement at the LOWEST cost?
options: EC2 Dedicated Hosts allocated in the Region
EC2 Dedicated Instances launched in the VPC
EC2 instances in a cluster placement group
EC2 On-Demand Instances with enhanced networking
explanation: Dedicated Instances run on single-tenant hardware but AWS controls placement and you get no socket visibility, which is all this requirement needs. Dedicated Hosts add physical-server visibility and placement control at higher cost, which only socket-bound licensing justifies.
distractors: Dedicated Hosts also isolate hardware but reserve an entire physical server; they cost more and their extra visibility is only needed for per-socket/per-core licences.
Placement groups control proximity for latency; they say nothing about tenancy.
Default tenancy shares hosts with other customers, whatever the networking option.

stem: A company must route all inbound and outbound traffic for several VPCs through a fleet of third-party next-generation firewall appliances, transparently and at scale, without changing application code. Which load balancer should front the appliances?
options: Application Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
explanation: Gateway Load Balancer operates at layer 3 with GENEVE encapsulation, steering traffic transparently through third-party virtual appliances and scaling them like any other target group.
distractors: An ALB terminates HTTP and routes on content; it cannot pass raw IP packets through inspection appliances.
An NLB balances TCP/UDP connections to targets; it does not transparently insert appliances into the packet path.
The Classic Load Balancer is legacy layer 4/7 balancing and has no appliance-insertion capability.

stem: A Network Load Balancer spans two Availability Zones with eight targets in AZ-a and two in AZ-b. Monitoring shows the two AZ-b targets are heavily overloaded while AZ-a targets are idle. Which setting explains this and what should be done?
options: Enable sticky sessions so connections are pinned to the less busy AZ
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the NLB, which is off by default
Increase the deregistration delay so AZ-b targets drain slowly
Switch the health check to HTTP so overloaded targets are removed
explanation: Without cross-zone load balancing each NLB node distributes only to targets in its own AZ, so half the traffic lands on the two AZ-b targets. Cross-zone balancing is always on for ALB but off by default (and chargeable) for NLB.
distractors: Stickiness pins clients to targets; it does not rebalance traffic across AZs and would worsen skew.
Deregistration delay affects how long in-flight requests get to finish on a target being removed; it has nothing to do with distribution.
Health checks remove unhealthy targets; the AZ-b targets are healthy but overloaded because of the distribution rule.

stem: A SaaS platform serves twelve customer-branded domains from one Application Load Balancer, each with its own TLS certificate. Certificates keep expiring and causing outages. Which approach is the MOST operationally efficient?
options: Buy a single wildcard certificate covering all customer domains from a third-party CA and upload it to IAM
Create one ALB per domain, each with its own manually renewed certificate
Use ACM certificates for each domain, attached to one HTTPS listener using SNI, so renewal is automatic
Terminate TLS on the EC2 instances instead of on the load balancer
explanation: ACM issues certificates free of charge and renews them automatically when used on ELB, CloudFront or API Gateway. SNI lets a single ALB listener present a different certificate depending on the hostname requested.
distractors: A wildcard cannot cover unrelated customer domains, and third-party certificates must still be renewed and re-uploaded manually.
Twelve load balancers multiply cost and the manual renewal burden remains.
Terminating on instances moves the renewal problem onto every instance and loses the ACM auto-renewal benefit.

stem: An Auto Scaling group behind an ALB serves short API requests that complete in under a second. During scale-in, instances stay in the Terminating state for about five minutes before they are removed, delaying cost savings. Which change reduces this delay safely?
options: Lower the target group's deregistration delay from the default 300 seconds to a few seconds
Disable the ELB health checks on the Auto Scaling group and rely on EC2 status checks instead
Set the Auto Scaling group's default cooldown to zero so scale-in activities finish sooner
Enable sticky sessions on the target group so in-flight requests finish on the same instance
explanation: Deregistration delay (connection draining) holds a target in service for in-flight requests before removal, defaulting to 300 seconds. With sub-second requests it can be reduced dramatically without dropping traffic.
distractors: Health check type affects which instances get replaced, not how long draining takes.
Cooldown governs how soon another scaling activity may start; it does not shorten the draining wait.
Stickiness would tend to keep connections on a draining target longer, not shorter.

stem: A web tier runs in an Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones with a minimum of 1, desired 1 and maximum 6 behind an Application Load Balancer. During an AZ outage the site was unavailable for several minutes. The company wants to be resilient to a single AZ failure at the LOWEST additional cost. Which change meets these requirements?
options: Set the minimum and desired capacity to 2 so that one instance runs in each Availability Zone
Add a third Availability Zone to the group and keep the minimum capacity at 1 to limit the additional cost
Set the maximum capacity to 12 so that the group can replace a lost instance more quickly
Change the single instance to a larger instance type so that it can absorb the traffic
explanation: With min 1 the only instance may be in the failed AZ, and the site is down until the replacement boots elsewhere. Minimum two spread over two AZs means one survives the outage, at the cost of one extra instance.
distractors: A third AZ with a single instance still leaves the whole tier in one AZ at any moment.
Raising max changes how far the group can grow, not what is running when the AZ fails.
A larger single instance is still one instance in one AZ.

stem: An API tier scales on average CPU utilisation, but the application is I/O-bound: it saturates on concurrent requests while CPU stays around 30 percent, so the group never scales out and latency climbs. Which target tracking metric is a better fit?
options: ASGAverageNetworkIn averaged across the group
EBS volume read latency per instance
GroupDesiredCapacity for the group
ALBRequestCountPerTarget for the group
explanation: For request-bound applications, request count per target tracks the actual load each instance handles and is a leading indicator; CPU is lagging and misleading when the bottleneck is not compute.
distractors: Network bytes in is only loosely related to request concurrency and depends on payload size.
Disk latency is a symptom on a single volume; it is not a group-level target tracking metric for web request load.
GroupDesiredCapacity is an output of scaling, not a load signal to scale on.

stem: An engineer needs to investigate an instance in an Auto Scaling group that is intermittently failing its ELB health check, but every time it is marked unhealthy the group terminates it before the investigation can finish. What should the engineer do to keep the instance alive temporarily?
options: Set the health check grace period to zero so the group re-evaluates the instance immediately
Change the health check type from ELB to EC2 permanently so only hardware failures count
Suspend the ReplaceUnhealthy process on the Auto Scaling group while the investigation runs
Detach the Application Load Balancer from the group until the investigation has finished
explanation: Suspending the ReplaceUnhealthy (or Terminate) process tells the group to stop replacing instances it considers unhealthy, so the engineer can debug in place and resume the process afterwards.
distractors: A zero grace period makes the group act on health checks sooner, the opposite of what is needed.
Switching to EC2 checks would stop the replacement but also permanently reintroduces the problem of running-but-broken instances staying in service.
Detaching the load balancer removes traffic from the whole tier; it is far more disruptive than pausing one process.

stem: After a database connectivity fault on one instance, users behind an ALB intermittently received errors for an hour, yet all targets stayed healthy the whole time. The target group health check points at /index.html, a static page. What should be changed?
options: Increase the healthy threshold count so that instances are marked healthy more slowly after a failed check
Point the health check at an endpoint such as /health that exercises the application's database dependency
Switch the health check protocol from HTTP to TCP so the check completes faster and more often
Enable access logs on the Application Load Balancer and alarm on the number of 5xx responses
explanation: A health check only detects what it tests. A static page proves the web server is up, not that the app can serve real requests; a health route that touches the database lets the ALB (and an ASG using ELB health checks) remove the broken instance.
distractors: Thresholds tune how quickly state changes; the check itself never fails here, so thresholds are irrelevant.
A TCP check is even shallower than an HTTP request for a static file.
Access logs give a record of requests for later analysis; they do not affect routing decisions.

stem: A Lambda function writes to a small RDS instance. During traffic surges the function scales to hundreds of concurrent executions and exhausts the database's connection limit, causing failures for other applications sharing the database. Which setting limits the damage with the LEAST change?
options: Enable provisioned concurrency on the function so that warm environments reuse connections
Configure reserved concurrency on the function to cap its maximum concurrent executions
Increase the function's memory allocation so each invocation releases its connection sooner
Raise the account's Regional concurrency quota so the surge is absorbed without throttling
explanation: Reserved concurrency both guarantees and caps how much of the account's concurrency pool a function may use. Capping it protects the downstream database from being overwhelmed; excess invocations are throttled instead.
distractors: Provisioned Concurrency keeps environments warm to remove cold starts; it does not cap scaling.
Faster invocations do not bound how many run at once during a surge.
A larger quota lets the function scale further and would make the connection exhaustion worse.

stem: A data science team wants to run inference in Lambda, but their function with its machine-learning libraries is about 1.5 GB unzipped and deployment fails. Which approach lets them keep using Lambda?
options: Split the libraries across several Lambda layers
Request a quota increase for the zip deployment package size
Store the libraries in S3 and download them into /tmp on every invocation
Package the function as a container image stored in Amazon ECR
explanation: Zip-based deployments are limited to 250 MB unzipped including layers, but container image packaging supports images up to 10 GB, which is the documented route for large ML dependencies.
distractors: Layers count toward the same 250 MB unzipped limit, so splitting does not raise the ceiling.
The 250 MB unzipped limit for zip packages is not adjustable; the container image path is the supported answer.
Downloading 1.5 GB into ephemeral storage on each cold start adds huge latency and cost and may exceed the default /tmp size.

stem: An ECS service on Fargate starts successfully and pulls its image from ECR, but the application inside the container receives AccessDenied when it tries to write to an S3 bucket. Which role must be changed?
options: The task execution role, which needs s3:PutObject on the bucket
The ECS service-linked role, which needs s3:PutObject on the bucket added to its policy
The task role in the task definition, which needs s3:PutObject on the bucket
The instance profile of the container hosts, which needs s3:PutObject
explanation: The task role is what the application code assumes to call AWS services. The task execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull images and push logs, and since the task started, that role is already fine.
distractors: The execution role covers ECR pulls and CloudWatch Logs; the application's SDK calls do not use it.
The service-linked role lets ECS manage load balancers and networking on your behalf, not application access to S3.
Fargate has no customer-managed hosts, so there is no instance profile to configure.

stem: A startup exposes a Lambda-backed public API and wants the cheapest API Gateway option, but must issue each partner an API key with a per-partner request quota and be able to cache responses. Which API type meets the requirements?
options: HTTP API, because it is around 70 percent cheaper and supports Lambda proxy integrations
REST API, because usage plans with API keys and response caching are only available there
WebSocket API, because it supports per-connection quotas and persistent partner sessions
HTTP API with a Lambda authorizer that enforces the per-partner quotas and caches responses
explanation: HTTP APIs are cheaper and lower-latency, but API keys with usage plans and stage-level caching are REST API features. When the question requires them, the REST API is the right choice despite the higher price.
distractors: The cost saving is real, but HTTP APIs do not offer usage plans, API keys or response caching.
WebSocket APIs are for stateful two-way connections and do not provide usage plans or caching for a request/response API.
A custom authorizer can validate tokens but building metering, quotas and caching yourself is more work and still misses native caching.

stem: A loan approval process runs several Lambda functions in sequence, waits up to five business days for a human reviewer to approve, then continues. Each application must be processed exactly once. Which service should orchestrate it?
options: A single long-running Lambda function that polls for the approval
An SQS FIFO queue with a visibility timeout of five days
Step Functions Standard workflow
Step Functions Express workflow
explanation: Standard workflows run for up to a year with exactly-once execution semantics and support waiting for human approval via callback tasks. Express workflows are capped at five minutes and are at-least-once.
distractors: Lambda's 15-minute limit rules out anything that waits days.
SQS visibility timeouts max out at 12 hours, and a queue does not orchestrate multi-step branching logic.
Express workflows are limited to five minutes and offer at-least-once semantics, wrong on both counts.

stem: A nightly reporting job runs for about three hours, is fault-tolerant and can be retried, and currently runs on an always-on EC2 instance. The company wants the LOWEST cost with minimal operational overhead. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Split the job into 15-minute chunks and run each chunk as a Lambda function on a schedule
Run the job on AWS Batch with Spot capacity, triggered by a nightly EventBridge schedule
Keep the EC2 instance and purchase a three-year Reserved Instance to reduce its hourly cost
Deploy the job to Elastic Beanstalk in a single-instance environment with a nightly cron entry
explanation: The job exceeds Lambda's 15-minute limit, so managed batch compute is the fit; AWS Batch queues and runs it on Spot capacity, so you pay heavily discounted rates for only three hours a night rather than a 24/7 instance.
distractors: Forcing a three-hour job into 15-minute chunks adds engineering complexity and checkpoint plumbing to work around a limit that Batch simply does not have.
An RI discounts a machine that still idles 21 hours a day; paying only while the job runs is cheaper.
Beanstalk still runs an always-on instance and is aimed at web applications, not scheduled batch jobs.

stem: A media company keeps medical-imaging archives in S3. Images are rarely opened, but when a clinician requests one it must load in milliseconds. Objects are kept for years. Which storage class is MOST cost-effective?
options: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
S3 Standard
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval is priced as an archive tier but still returns objects in milliseconds, which is exactly the 'rarely accessed but must be instant' combination.
distractors: Deep Archive needs 12 to 48 hours to restore, so a clinician would wait half a day.
Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours to restore; it fails the millisecond requirement.
Standard meets the latency but is far more expensive for data that is rarely read.

stem: An analytics pipeline writes millions of small JSON files (about 20 KB each) to S3 every day. Files are read heavily for a week and almost never afterwards, but must be retained for one year. A lifecycle rule transitions them to Standard-IA after 7 days, yet the bill barely changed. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: Objects smaller than 128 KB are not transitioned to Standard-IA by default because it would cost more
Lifecycle transitions require S3 Intelligent-Tiering to be enabled on the bucket before any rule runs
Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum duration, so transitions before day 30 are silently delayed
Lifecycle rules only run on buckets with versioning enabled, and versioning is off on this bucket
explanation: S3 does not transition objects under 128 KB to the IA classes by default; small objects would cost more in IA (per-object minimum billable size and request charges) than in Standard, so the rule has nothing to act on.
distractors: Intelligent-Tiering is a storage class, not a prerequisite for lifecycle rules.
Transitioning to IA before day 30 is allowed; the object simply incurs the minimum-duration charge if deleted early. It is not silently delayed.
Lifecycle rules work on unversioned buckets too.

stem: A company enables Cross-Region Replication from a bucket in eu-west-1 to a new bucket in us-east-1 for disaster recovery. A week later they notice the destination only contains objects uploaded after the rule was created. What should they do to copy the pre-existing 40 TB with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Enable S3 Replication Time Control on the rule
Create a second replication rule with a filter matching the older prefixes
Run S3 Batch Replication for the existing objects
Write a script that re-uploads every object so the replication rule fires
explanation: Replication rules only act on objects written after the rule exists. S3 Batch Replication is the managed way to replicate the existing inventory of a bucket to the destination.
distractors: RTC adds a 15-minute replication SLA for new objects; it does not backfill existing ones.
New rules, whatever their filter, still only apply to objects written after they exist.
Re-uploading 40 TB works but is expensive, slow and something you have to build and babysit.

stem: A financial firm must guarantee that trade confirmations stored in S3 cannot be deleted or overwritten for five years by anyone, including account administrators, and must be able to prove it to auditors. Which configuration meets this requirement?
options: A bucket policy denying s3:DeleteObject to all principals
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a five-year retention period
Versioning with MFA Delete enabled on the bucket
S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a five-year retention period
explanation: Compliance mode is the only mode where the retention period cannot be shortened or the object deleted by any user, including the root account, until it expires. That is what 'nobody, including administrators' asks for.
distractors: A bucket policy can be edited by an administrator; it is not a WORM guarantee.
MFA Delete stops casual deletions but a user with MFA and root credentials can still delete or suspend versioning.
Governance mode can be bypassed by principals holding s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, so an administrator can still delete.

stem: A data-lake bucket is shared by product teams in twenty AWS accounts. Each team must write only to its own prefix, and each team's access must be allowed only from that team's VPC. The single bucket policy has become unmanageable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create an S3 access point per team, restricted to the team's VPC, with an access-point policy scoped to its prefix
Grant per-team access with object ACLs on each prefix and reference the team's VPC in the ACL grants
Move the permissions into twenty IAM groups in the bucket owner's account that reference the same bucket ARN
Split the data into twenty buckets, one per team, each with a bucket policy that allows access only from that team's VPC endpoint
explanation: S3 access points give each consumer a named endpoint with its own policy and an optional network origin of a single VPC, so both the prefix scope and the VPC restriction live with the access point while the bucket policy stays small.
distractors: ACLs are legacy, disabled by default with Bucket Owner Enforced, and cannot express a prefix or a VPC condition.
IAM groups exist in one account; cross-account teams cannot be members, and the bucket policy is the artefact that needs shrinking.
Twenty buckets breaks the data-lake model and multiplies replication, logging and lifecycle configuration.

stem: A regulated workload requires that every object written to a bucket is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, that key usage is auditable in CloudTrail, and that KMS request charges are kept as low as possible. Which TWO actions should the architect take? (Choose TWO.)
options: Set the bucket's default encryption to SSE-S3
Require SSE-C so the application supplies the key on every request
Encrypt client-side with the AWS Encryption SDK before upload
Set the bucket's default encryption to SSE-KMS with the customer-managed key
Enable S3 Bucket Keys on the bucket
explanation: SSE-KMS with a customer-managed key gives key policies, rotation and a CloudTrail audit trail of key usage; S3 Bucket Keys derive a bucket-level data key so KMS API calls (and their cost) drop by up to 99%.
distractors: SSE-S3 uses AWS-managed keys with no key policy and no per-request CloudTrail record of key usage.
SSE-C keeps keys outside AWS entirely; KMS is not involved, so there is no KMS audit trail.
Client-side encryption also bypasses KMS auditing on S3's side and moves key handling into every client.

stem: An ingestion service writes several thousand small objects per second to one S3 bucket. All keys start with the same date prefix, such as ingest/2026-09-15/<uuid>, and the service now receives 503 Slow Down responses during peaks. What is the MOST effective fix?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket so requests are served from edge locations
Move the objects to S3 Express One Zone, which supports a higher request rate per bucket
Distribute the keys across multiple prefixes so that requests are parallelised
Turn on S3 Intelligent-Tiering so that frequently written objects move to a faster tier
explanation: S3 scales to at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per prefix. Spreading writes across several prefixes multiplies that headroom; a single date prefix concentrates every write on one partition.
distractors: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance uploads via edge locations; it does not lift per-prefix request limits.
Express One Zone is for very low latency in one AZ and requires migrating data and code; prefix partitioning fixes the throttling directly.
Intelligent-Tiering is about storage cost tiers and does not change request throughput.

stem: A research institute publishes a 500 TB open dataset in S3. Thousands of external users download it, and the institute's data-transfer bill is now larger than its storage bill. The data must stay in S3 and remain available to anyone with an AWS account. What should the institute do to reduce its cost?
options: Move the dataset to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Enable Requester Pays on the bucket
Serve the dataset through S3 Transfer Acceleration
Compress the objects and enable S3 Select
explanation: With Requester Pays enabled, the requester's AWS account is billed for the data transfer and requests instead of the bucket owner. This is the documented pattern for sharing large datasets.
distractors: Deep Archive cuts storage cost but makes downloads take hours and does nothing about egress charges.
Transfer Acceleration adds an extra per-GB fee on top of transfer; it increases cost.
S3 Select reduces bytes for queries that need a subset, but the users download whole objects; it does not shift the cost.

stem: A team uploads multi-gigabyte video files to S3 using multipart upload from unreliable field connections. Their storage bill is higher than the total size of the objects listed in the bucket. What is the MOST likely cause, and how should it be fixed?
options: S3 Standard has a minimum billable object size, so move the objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Transfer Acceleration is being billed for each upload, so disable it on the bucket
Versioning is retaining previous copies of each file, so suspend versioning on the bucket
Incomplete multipart uploads are consuming storage, so add a lifecycle rule to abort them
explanation: Parts of an upload that never completes are stored and billed but never appear as objects. A lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads after N days removes them.
distractors: Standard has no minimum billable size (that is the IA classes) and the issue is invisible parts, not per-object minimums.
Transfer Acceleration is a per-GB transfer fee, not storage, and the question describes storage cost.
Old versions would appear in a versioned listing; nothing here says versioning is on, and unreliable connections point at abandoned parts.

stem: A company runs an event-driven pipeline: each CSV uploaded to a bucket must trigger processing, and the team also wants to route notifications to several targets, filter on object metadata, and archive the events. Which approach offers the MOST flexibility with the LEAST custom code?
options: Send S3 events to Amazon EventBridge and create rules per target
Poll the bucket with a scheduled Lambda listing new keys
Enable S3 Inventory and process the daily report
Configure S3 Event Notifications to publish to a single SQS queue and fan out from consumers
explanation: Routing S3 events through EventBridge gives content-based filtering, many rule targets, archiving and replay without writing fan-out code.
distractors: Polling adds latency and cost and does not scale with millions of objects.
Inventory is a daily report for auditing storage, not a real-time event source.
A single SQS target works but multi-target routing and metadata filtering then become code you own.

stem: An application uses a 2 TB gp2 volume that was sized to reach 6,000 IOPS even though it stores only 300 GB of data. Which change reduces cost while keeping the same IOPS?
options: Switch to a 300 GB io2 volume provisioned at 6,000 IOPS to pay only for the used capacity
Switch to a 300 GB gp3 volume and provision 6,000 IOPS independently of the volume size
Switch to a 2 TB st1 volume, which delivers the same IOPS at a lower price per GB
Keep the gp2 volume but enable EBS optimisation on the instance to raise its IOPS
explanation: gp3 decouples IOPS and throughput from capacity: 3,000 IOPS baseline is included and more can be provisioned without buying storage. It is also about 20% cheaper per GB than gp2.
distractors: io2 delivers the IOPS but at a much higher price per provisioned IOPS; gp3 is the cost answer.
st1 is a throughput-optimised HDD with a few hundred IOPS; it cannot deliver 6,000 IOPS.
EBS optimisation affects the instance's dedicated bandwidth, not the volume's IOPS or the amount of storage billed.

stem: A log-processing job reads multi-terabyte files sequentially from EBS at high throughput; IOPS are irrelevant, and the volume is a data disk, not the root volume. Which volume type is MOST cost-effective while meeting the throughput need?
options: gp3
io2 Block Express
st1
sc1
explanation: st1 (throughput-optimised HDD) is built for large sequential workloads and delivers up to 500 MB/s at a low per-GB price. It cannot be a boot volume, which is fine here.
distractors: gp3 caps at 1,000 MB/s but you pay SSD prices for a workload that only needs sequential throughput.
io2 Block Express is for high random IOPS and sub-millisecond latency; overkill and expensive.
sc1 is cheaper still but is for cold, rarely accessed data at 250 MB/s; the job needs sustained throughput.

stem: A database on EC2 in eu-west-1 stores data on an unencrypted EBS volume. Compliance now requires the volume to be encrypted at rest and a copy of the data to be kept in eu-central-1 for disaster recovery. Which TWO steps are part of the correct approach? (Choose TWO.)
options: Enable encryption on the existing volume from the console
Snapshot the volume and copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, then create a new volume from the encrypted copy and swap it in
Copy the snapshot to eu-central-1
Detach the volume and attach it to an instance in eu-central-1
Enable EBS default encryption in the account so existing volumes are re-encrypted
explanation: You cannot encrypt a volume in place. The snapshot → copy-with-encryption → new-volume path encrypts it, and copying the snapshot cross-Region is how EBS data reaches another Region for DR.
distractors: An existing volume cannot be toggled to encrypted.
EBS volumes are zonal and cannot be attached across AZs, let alone Regions.
Default encryption only affects newly created volumes and snapshots; existing volumes stay as they are.

stem: A distributed search engine on EC2 keeps its indexes on local disks and replicates every shard to two other nodes. Nodes need the highest possible disk IOPS. Which storage should each node use?
options: io2 Block Express EBS volumes
EFS with Max I/O performance mode
gp3 EBS volumes with maximum provisioned IOPS
Instance store volumes
explanation: Instance store is NVMe on the host and gives the highest IOPS available; its ephemerality is acceptable because the application already replicates shards across nodes.
distractors: io2 Block Express is durable and fast, but a system that replicates itself does not need the durability and instance store is faster and included in the instance price.
EFS is a shared network filesystem with higher latency; it is the wrong shape for local index storage.
gp3 tops out at 16,000 IOPS, well below local NVMe.

stem: A Linux fleet in three AZs shares an EFS filesystem. During peak load, thousands of instances read and write in parallel and aggregate throughput, not per-operation latency, is the bottleneck. Which EFS setting should the architect change?
options: Switch to EFS One Zone storage class
Change the performance mode to Max I/O
Change the throughput mode to Bursting
Mount using an EFS access point per instance
explanation: Max I/O performance mode scales to higher aggregate throughput and thousands of concurrent clients at the cost of slightly higher per-operation latency, which the scenario says is acceptable.
distractors: One Zone lowers cost and durability; it does not raise throughput and would break the three-AZ design.
Bursting throughput ties throughput to stored size and can throttle; Elastic or Provisioned would be the throughput answers, and the question points at parallelism.
Access points scope permissions and root directories; they do not change performance.

stem: A team stores build artefacts on EFS. Most files are read for a few days after creation and then untouched for months, but occasionally an old file is needed. The EFS bill keeps growing. What is the MOST cost-effective change with no application modification?
options: Switch the file system to Provisioned throughput mode sized for the average read load
Migrate the share to FSx for Lustre and link it to an S3 bucket for the old artefacts
Enable EFS lifecycle management to move untouched files to Infrequent Access
Copy files older than 30 days to S3 Glacier with a cron job and delete them from EFS
explanation: EFS lifecycle management transitions files not accessed for a configured period to the Infrequent Access (or Archive) class transparently; the path stays the same and files remain readable.
distractors: Provisioned throughput usually costs more, not less; it is a performance setting.
FSx for Lustre is a high-performance filesystem and is not cheaper for cold artefacts.
Copying to Glacier changes access paths and needs code; occasionally needed files would then take hours to restore.

stem: A company is migrating an on-premises NetApp storage array to AWS. Linux applications mount it over NFS while Windows applications use SMB, and administrators rely on snapshots and thin clones. Which service should they migrate to?
options: Amazon FSx for Lustre
Amazon EFS
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
explanation: FSx for NetApp ONTAP is multi-protocol (NFS, SMB, iSCSI) and preserves ONTAP features such as snapshots, cloning and deduplication, which makes it the drop-in target for a NetApp estate.
distractors: Lustre is a parallel HPC filesystem, not a general multi-protocol file share.
EFS is NFS only and does not serve SMB to Windows clients.
FSx for Windows is SMB and Active Directory focused; it does not natively serve NFS to Linux clients with ONTAP-style cloning.

stem: An on-premises backup team must retire its tape library. The existing backup software must keep running unchanged and backups must land in AWS at the lowest storage cost. What should the architect propose?
options: AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway with virtual tapes archived to Glacier
AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway exposing an NFS share to the backup servers
AWS Snowball Edge devices shipped to AWS at the end of every month
AWS DataSync scheduled nightly from the backup servers to an S3 bucket
explanation: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library to existing backup software (iSCSI VTL) and stores tapes in S3, archiving ejected tapes to Glacier tiers, so nothing changes on the software side.
distractors: File Gateway is a file share, so again the backup software must change from tape to file targets.
Snowball is for bulk one-off migration, not an ongoing tape workflow.
DataSync copies files; the backup software would need reconfiguring to write files rather than tapes.

stem: A company must migrate 8 TB of files from an on-premises NAS to Amazon EFS within a week. It has an idle 1 Gbps internet connection and wants data validated on arrival. Which approach is MOST cost-effective?
options: Use S3 Transfer Acceleration then copy from S3 to EFS
Order a Snowball Edge device
Use AWS DataSync from an on-premises agent to the EFS filesystem
Set up Storage Gateway File Gateway and copy the files through it
explanation: At roughly 10 TB per day over 1 Gbps, 8 TB is comfortably under a week's window. DataSync copies directly to EFS with built-in validation and encryption and needs no hardware.
distractors: Transfer Acceleration is an S3 upload feature; going via S3 adds a second copy step for no benefit.
Snowball makes sense at tens to hundreds of TB or when bandwidth is poor; for 8 TB over an idle 1 Gbps link it is slower and costlier.
File Gateway targets S3, not EFS, and is a persistent hybrid share rather than a migration tool.

stem: A team is designing a VPC that will later peer with a partner network using 10.0.0.0/16. They also need a subnet with at least 200 usable addresses per AZ. Which design is correct?
options: VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with /24 subnets
VPC 172.16.0.0/16 with /24 subnets
VPC 10.0.0.0/16 with /28 subnets
VPC 172.16.0.0/16 with /28 subnets
explanation: The VPC CIDR must not overlap the partner's 10.0.0.0/16, so pick a different private range. A /24 has 256 addresses minus 5 reserved by AWS, giving 251 usable, which covers 200.
distractors: 10.0.0.0/16 overlaps the partner network, so peering can never be established.
Overlaps the partner and a /28 gives only 11 usable addresses.
No overlap, but a /28 has 16 addresses minus 5 reserved, far short of 200.

stem: An EC2 instance is launched into a subnet whose route table has 0.0.0.0/0 pointing at an Internet Gateway, and its security group allows inbound SSH from the office. Administrators still cannot connect. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The instance has no public IPv4 or Elastic IP address
The VPC's local route was accidentally deleted
The security group needs an outbound rule for SSH replies
The subnet is in an AZ that does not support Internet Gateways
explanation: A subnet is public because of its route, but the instance itself still needs a public IPv4 or Elastic IP to be reached from the internet. Public route plus private-only IP means no inbound connectivity.
distractors: The local route is implicit and cannot be removed.
Security groups are stateful; replies to allowed inbound traffic are automatically permitted.
Internet Gateways are VPC-wide and work in every AZ.

stem: A company runs application servers in private subnets across three AZs, all routing 0.0.0.0/0 to a single NAT Gateway in AZ-a. During an AZ-a outage, servers in AZ-b and AZ-c lose internet access. What should the architect change?
options: Move the NAT gateway into a private subnet so that it is no longer affected by the outage
Attach a second internet gateway to the VPC so that egress has a redundant path
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance in each Availability Zone
Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and point each private route table at its own AZ's gateway
explanation: NAT Gateways are zonal. One per AZ, each referenced by that AZ's private route table, removes the single point of failure and also avoids cross-AZ data charges.
distractors: A NAT Gateway must sit in a public subnet with a route to the IGW; moving it to a private subnet breaks it and does nothing for AZ isolation.
A VPC has exactly one Internet Gateway; the IGW is not the failing component.
NAT instances add self-managed HA and lower throughput; NAT Gateway per AZ is the managed answer.

stem: An analytics fleet in private subnets pulls terabytes per day from S3 and DynamoDB and makes high-volume calls to Kinesis Data Streams and SQS. NAT Gateway data-processing charges dominate the bill. Which TWO changes reduce it? (Choose TWO.)
options: Add Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB and route the private subnets to them
Replace the NAT Gateway with a NAT instance on a large EC2 type
Add Interface VPC endpoints for Kinesis Data Streams and SQS
Enable IPv6 and use an Egress-only Internet Gateway
Move the fleet to public subnets so it uses the Internet Gateway directly
explanation: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and take the bulk traffic off the NAT entirely; for other AWS services an interface endpoint's hourly plus per-GB price is usually well below NAT processing charges at volume.
distractors: A NAT instance shifts cost to EC2 hours and bandwidth and adds operational risk; the traffic still flows through it.
IPv6 egress requires dual-stack endpoints and does not remove the fact that traffic leaves the VPC; the endpoints are the direct fix.
Public subnets require a public IP on every instance (each now billed) and expose the fleet; still pays internet egress.

stem: A three-tier application has an ALB, an Auto Scaling group of application instances, and an RDS MySQL database in private subnets. Instances scale in and out frequently. How should the database security group be configured so that ONLY application instances can connect on port 3306?
options: Add a NACL rule on the database subnet allowing 3306 from each instance IP
Allow 3306 from the application subnets' CIDR ranges
Allow 3306 from the application tier's security group
Allow 3306 from 0.0.0.0/0 and rely on the private subnet for isolation
explanation: Security groups can reference other security groups. Allowing 3306 from the app tier's SG keeps working as instances launch and terminate, and grants nothing to other resources that happen to share the subnet.
distractors: Per-IP NACL rules break as soon as Auto Scaling replaces an instance and NACLs cannot reference security groups.
CIDR rules admit anything else in those subnets, such as a bastion or a misplaced instance.
Private subnets are not an isolation boundary; anything in the VPC could reach the database.

stem: After a custom network ACL was applied to a public subnet, users report that HTTPS connections to a web server open but then hang and time out. The security group allows inbound 443 and all outbound. What is the fix?
options: Change the network ACL to allow inbound port 80 as well as port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
Enable the enableDnsHostnames attribute on the VPC so clients can resolve the server
Add an outbound security group rule for port 443 so the server can send its responses
Add an outbound network ACL rule allowing TCP 1024-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0
explanation: NACLs are stateless. The request arrives on 443, but the server's replies go back to the client's ephemeral port and are dropped unless an outbound rule allows the 1024-65535 range. 'Works one way then hangs' is the NACL signature.
distractors: Port 80 is unrelated; the 443 connection opens, so inbound is fine — the replies are dropped.
DNS attributes affect name resolution, not the flow of established connections.
The security group already allows all outbound and is stateful anyway; it is not the culprit.

stem: A security team has identified a single IP address performing credential-stuffing attacks against EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer. The team must block that address at the network layer without affecting other traffic. What should they do?
options: Add a low-numbered deny rule for that IP to the subnet's network ACL
Remove the public IP addresses from the instances behind the load balancer
Configure the NLB listener with a rule that rejects requests from that source IP
Add a deny rule for that IP to the security group attached to the instances
explanation: Only NACLs can express deny. A low rule number ensures the deny is evaluated before any allow rule that would otherwise match. Security groups are allow-only.
distractors: Removing public IPs breaks the service for every user, not just the attacker.
NLB listeners forward at layer 4 and have no source-IP block list; NACLs (or WAF at layer 7 in front of ALB/CloudFront) do.
Security groups have no deny rules; you can only omit allows, and inbound from the internet is already allowed by design.

stem: A company has a Route 53 private hosted zone for internal.example.com associated with a VPC. Instances in that VPC cannot resolve names in the zone, though public DNS works. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The security group on the instances blocks outbound UDP 53 to the Amazon-provided resolver
The hosted zone must be public for instances in the VPC to be able to query it
The VPC does not have both enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames enabled
The instances need a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint to reach the private zone
explanation: Private hosted zones require both VPC DNS attributes to be enabled; with either off, the Amazon-provided resolver will not answer for the private zone.
distractors: Security groups do not filter traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS at VPC+2 for standard queries.
Private hosted zones are exactly for internal names resolved inside associated VPCs.
Inbound Resolver endpoints let on-premises resolvers query VPC names; instances inside the VPC use the VPC+2 resolver directly.

stem: An on-premises Active Directory domain must be resolvable from EC2 instances, and on-premises servers must resolve names in a Route 53 private hosted zone. A Site-to-Site VPN is already in place. Which TWO components are required? (Choose TWO.)
options: Conditional forwarders configured on each EC2 instance pointing at the on-premises DNS servers
enableDnsHostnames disabled on the VPC so queries leave the VPC
A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for the on-premises domain
A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint that on-premises DNS servers forward the private zone to
A public hosted zone containing both sets of records
explanation: Outbound endpoints plus forwarding rules let the VPC resolver send queries for on-prem domains to on-prem DNS; inbound endpoints give on-prem DNS an IP inside the VPC to forward queries for the private zone to.
distractors: Per-instance forwarders are unmanageable and break with Auto Scaling; the Resolver endpoints do this centrally.
Both DNS attributes must be enabled for private hosted zones to resolve; disabling one breaks resolution.
Publishing internal AD and private zone records publicly is insecure and does not integrate the on-prem AD.

stem: After a suspected intrusion, an investigator needs to know which source IPs attempted connections to a specific instance's ENI over the past week and whether they were accepted or rejected. Which data source answers this?
options: VPC Flow Logs on the ENI
AWS Config configuration history
Traffic Mirroring session recordings
CloudTrail management events
explanation: Flow Logs record connection metadata (source, destination, ports, ACCEPT/REJECT) at VPC, subnet or ENI level, delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose. This is the 'what was rejected and by whom' answer.
distractors: Config tracks resource configuration changes, not traffic.
Traffic Mirroring captures full packets in real time for an appliance; it must be running beforehand and is not a week-long log of accepts and rejects.
CloudTrail records API calls to AWS, not network connections to an instance.

stem: An instance in a private subnet cannot reach an RDS database in another subnet. The engineer suspects a misconfiguration but the VPC has dozens of route tables, NACLs and security groups. Which tool identifies the EXACT component blocking the path with the LEAST effort?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor
VPC Flow Logs queried in CloudWatch Logs Insights
AWS Network Firewall logs
VPC Reachability Analyzer
explanation: Reachability Analyzer performs a static analysis of the path between two resources and names the specific route table, NACL or security group that blocks it, automating the route → NACL → SG debug walk.
distractors: Trusted Advisor flags broad best-practice issues, not a specific blocked path.
Flow Logs show REJECTs but not which of route, NACL or SG caused them; you would still have to walk the configuration.
Network Firewall only logs traffic that traverses it, which intra-VPC traffic typically does not.

stem: Review of a three-tier VPC finds: public subnets in two AZs with an ALB and one NAT Gateway; private application subnets in two AZs routing 0.0.0.0/0 to that NAT Gateway; private database subnets in two AZs with a route 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway 'so RDS can fetch updates'. Which TWO changes improve resilience and security? (Choose TWO.)
options: Attach an Elastic IP to each application instance
Add a second NAT Gateway in the other AZ and repoint that AZ's application route table to it
Move the RDS instances into the public subnets so they can reach the internet without NAT
Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 route from the database subnets; RDS is managed and needs no internet route
Replace the ALB with an NLB so it does not need public subnets
explanation: A single NAT Gateway is a single point of failure and a cross-AZ data charge; one per AZ fixes both. The data tier should have no internet route at all: RDS patching is done by AWS and an egress path only widens the blast radius.
distractors: Elastic IPs on private instances make them internet-addressable and add per-IP charges; the app tier should stay private behind NAT.
RDS in public subnets is the opposite of a secure data tier and does not need internet access.
An NLB still needs subnets and does not change the resilience of the NAT design.

stem: VPC A is peered with VPC B, and VPC B is peered with VPC C. Instances in VPC A cannot reach VPC C even though route tables in B point at both peerings. Why?
options: VPC C's CIDR overlaps VPC A's CIDR
Peering connections in different accounts cannot forward traffic
VPC peering is not transitive; A needs its own peering with C
Security groups in B must reference A's security group
explanation: Peering is strictly one-to-one. Traffic from A cannot transit B to reach C regardless of B's routes; A↔C needs a direct peering (or a Transit Gateway).
distractors: If CIDRs overlapped, the A–B or B–C peering itself could not exist; the described setup is possible, so overlap is not the reason.
Cross-account peering works fine; the issue is transitivity, not accounts.
Security group references only matter for the two peers of a connection and would not enable transit.

stem: Two VPCs in the same account and Region need to exchange traffic over private IPs. Their CIDRs do not overlap and no further VPCs will be added. Which is the MOST cost-effective option?
options: AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints in each direction
Site-to-Site VPN between the two VPCs
AWS Transit Gateway with two attachments
VPC peering connection
explanation: For a small, fixed number of VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs, peering is the simplest and cheapest: no hourly charge, only data transfer.
distractors: PrivateLink is one-directional per endpoint and billed per hour per AZ; it is for exposing a service, not general connectivity.
VPN between VPCs is unnecessary complexity and cost when peering is available.
Transit Gateway adds per-attachment hourly and per-GB charges that a two-VPC case does not justify.

stem: An organisation has 40 VPCs across 6 accounts. Every VPC must reach a shared-services VPC and on-premises via Direct Connect, but development VPCs must not be able to reach production VPCs. What is the MOST operationally efficient design?
options: A Transit Gateway shared via AWS RAM, with separate route tables for dev and prod attachments
AWS PrivateLink endpoints from every VPC to every other VPC and to the on-premises network
One Site-to-Site VPN per VPC to the on-premises router, with routes to the shared-services VPC
A full mesh of VPC peering connections with security groups that block dev-to-prod traffic
explanation: Transit Gateway is the hub for many VPCs, VPN and DX; RAM shares it across accounts, and TGW route tables give segmentation so spokes reach shared services but not each other.
distractors: PrivateLink exposes individual services one-directionally; it is not a routing fabric.
Per-VPC VPNs bypass the shared-services requirement and are far more to operate.
A 40-VPC mesh needs 780 peerings, is non-transitive to DX and cannot be centrally segmented.

stem: A company has a single 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection to its VPC. Management wants protection against a Direct Connect outage at the LOWEST cost, accepting reduced bandwidth during a failure. What should the architect propose?
options: Enable MACsec on the existing Direct Connect connection to protect the link
Order a second 10 Gbps Direct Connect connection at a different Direct Connect location for redundancy
Add a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet to the same virtual private gateway as a backup
Attach a second virtual private gateway to the VPC and associate the connection with it
explanation: A VPN as backup on the same VGW gives an independent path over the internet at low cost; BGP prefers Direct Connect while it is up and fails over to the VPN. Reduced bandwidth is accepted, so this is the intended cheap answer.
distractors: MACsec encrypts the link; it does not survive the link being cut.
A second DX gives full-bandwidth resilience but at roughly double the cost; the question asks for lowest cost.
A VPC has one VGW; the redundancy needed is in the path, not the gateway object.

stem: A healthcare provider connects to AWS over Direct Connect. An audit finds that traffic between the data centre and the VPC is not encrypted in transit and must be. Which TWO options satisfy the auditor while keeping the Direct Connect? (Choose TWO.)
options: Enable encryption on the private virtual interface
Run a Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect connection
Enable MACsec on the Direct Connect connection where the location supports it
Switch from a private VIF to a public VIF
Terminate the Direct Connect and use only a Site-to-Site VPN
explanation: Direct Connect is private but not encrypted by default. An IPsec VPN over the DX encrypts at layer 3, and MACsec (on supported dedicated connections) encrypts at layer 2; either adds encryption while keeping the dedicated path.
distractors: There is no encryption toggle on a VIF.
A public VIF reaches public AWS endpoints; it does not encrypt anything.
Dropping DX loses the consistent bandwidth and latency the company needs; encryption can be layered on top instead.

stem: A company already has a Direct Connect connection into a VPC in eu-west-1. It is now deploying VPCs in us-east-1 and ap-southeast-1 that must also be reachable from on-premises over the same Direct Connect. What should the architect add?
options: A Direct Connect gateway associated with the virtual private gateways in each Region
VPC peering from the eu-west-1 VPC to the other Regions, relying on transitive routing
A public virtual interface on the connection to reach the VPCs in the other Regions
A separate Direct Connect connection into each of the two new Regions
explanation: A Direct Connect Gateway lets one DX connection reach VPCs in multiple Regions through a private VIF, without additional physical connections.
distractors: Peering is non-transitive, so on-prem traffic arriving in eu-west-1 cannot hop onward.
A public VIF reaches public AWS endpoints, not the private IP space of VPCs.
Extra connections take weeks to months and cost port hours; DX Gateway makes them unnecessary.

stem: Lambda functions attached to private subnets must read from DynamoDB and write to S3. The VPC has no NAT gateway and no internet access, and the team wants to keep it that way at zero additional cost while ensuring the functions can reach only the company's own tables and buckets. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: A NAT gateway in a public subnet, restricted with a security group to the two services
A Transit Gateway attachment to a VPC that has internet access through its own NAT gateway
Interface endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in each private subnet with security groups
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB with endpoint policies naming the allowed resources
explanation: Gateway endpoints exist for exactly S3 and DynamoDB, are free, and work by adding a prefix-list route so traffic never leaves the AWS network. Each endpoint carries a policy that limits which buckets or tables are reachable through it.
distractors: NAT gateways cost hourly and per GB and would give general internet egress.
Routing through another VPC to the internet is complex, costly and defeats the private goal.
Interface endpoints work but are billed per hour per AZ and per GB; the gateway variant is free.

stem: On-premises servers connected via Direct Connect must upload to a specific S3 bucket without their traffic traversing the public internet, and the connection must resolve using S3's DNS names. Which solution works?
options: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 with its prefix list route propagated to the on-premises router
An interface VPC endpoint for S3 in the VPC, reached from on-premises over the private VIF
An S3 bucket policy that allows the on-premises CIDR range and denies everything else
S3 Transfer Acceleration enabled on the bucket, with uploads sent to the accelerated endpoint
explanation: Gateway endpoints are just a route inside the VPC and cannot be reached from on-premises. An interface endpoint has ENIs with private IPs in the VPC, so on-prem hosts over DX/VPN can reach S3 privately (a public VIF is the other option).
distractors: Gateway endpoint routes only apply to traffic originating in the VPC; on-prem hosts cannot use them.
A bucket policy authorises access; the traffic would still go over the public internet.
Transfer Acceleration uses public edge locations; it does not keep traffic private.

stem: A company sells an API hosted in its VPC and needs to make it privately available to hundreds of customer VPCs in other accounts. Many customers use the same 10.0.0.0/16 CIDR as the provider. Which approach meets the requirement?
options: Publish the API on an internet-facing ALB restricted by security groups to each customer's NAT IP
Establish VPC peering with each customer after asking them to re-address their overlapping VPCs
Expose the API behind a Network Load Balancer as a PrivateLink endpoint service for customers
Attach all customer VPCs to the provider's Transit Gateway and share it through AWS RAM
explanation: PrivateLink puts the service behind an NLB and consumers create interface endpoints in their own VPCs. Nothing is routed between the networks, so overlapping CIDRs are irrelevant and traffic stays one-directional and private.
distractors: Internet-facing exposure is not private, and NAT IP allow-lists are brittle.
Peering forbids overlapping CIDRs and asking hundreds of customers to re-address is not realistic.
Transit Gateway also requires non-overlapping CIDRs and gives customers broad network access rather than one service.

stem: A startup needs to connect its office to its VPC by the end of the week for developers to reach private resources. Traffic is light and must be encrypted, and budget is minimal. Which option should they pick?
options: AWS Transit Gateway with a Direct Connect Gateway
VPC peering to the office network
AWS Direct Connect hosted 1 Gbps connection
AWS Site-to-Site VPN to a Virtual Private Gateway
explanation: Site-to-Site VPN is provisioned in minutes, encrypted with IPsec, and cheap; it is the answer whenever the cue is 'quickly' and 'encrypted' with modest traffic.
distractors: TGW plus DX Gateway is enterprise-scale hybrid connectivity, expensive and slow to stand up.
Peering is between VPCs, not to an on-premises office.
Direct Connect takes weeks to months to provision and adds port-hour costs; wrong for a week's deadline and light traffic.

stem: A company's website at example.com must resolve to a CloudFront distribution. They also want to avoid per-query DNS charges where possible. Which Route 53 record should they create for the apex?
options: An alias A record pointing at the CloudFront distribution
An NS record delegating example.com to CloudFront
A CNAME record pointing at the distribution's domain name
An A record with the distribution's current IP addresses
explanation: Alias records work at the zone apex, track the AWS resource's changing IPs automatically, and alias queries to AWS resources are free.
distractors: NS delegation hands the zone to other name servers; CloudFront is not a DNS service.
CNAMEs are not permitted at the zone apex.
CloudFront's IPs change; hard-coding them will break.

stem: A team runs a web application in two Regions and wants to send 10% of users to a new version deployed in the second Region, increasing the share gradually while watching error rates. Which Route 53 routing policy should they use?
options: Latency-based routing
Failover routing
Weighted routing
Geoproximity routing with a bias
explanation: Weighted routing splits traffic by numeric weight, which is exactly the canary / gradual-migration pattern; setting a weight to 0 disables a target.
distractors: Latency routing sends users to whichever Region is fastest for them; you cannot dial a percentage.
Failover is active-passive; the secondary only receives traffic when the primary is unhealthy.
Geoproximity shifts traffic by geography and a bias, not by an explicit percentage across all users.

stem: A streaming service holds licences that allow certain content only for users in Japan. Users in Japan must always be served from ap-northeast-1 regardless of which Region would be fastest. Which routing policy is correct?
options: Latency-based routing
Geolocation routing
Multivalue answer routing
IP-based routing
explanation: Geolocation routes by the user's country or continent and enforces where traffic must go; it is the answer whenever the requirement is legal, licensing or residency rather than speed.
distractors: Latency routing may send a Japanese user to another Region if it measures faster, breaking the licence constraint.
Multivalue returns several healthy records at random; it does not consider location.
IP-based routing maps client CIDRs, which is for ISP-specific routing and impractical for a whole country.

stem: A company uses Route 53 failover records with health checks between a primary and a DR Region. During a test, users kept hitting the failed primary for several minutes after the health check turned unhealthy. What is the MOST likely reason and fix?
options: The record TTL is high, so resolvers cached the old answer; lower the TTL to about 60 seconds
Failover records require alias targets, so the plain A records must be converted to alias records first
The secondary record needs its own health check before Route 53 will return it to clients
The health check interval is too slow, so switch to Global Accelerator health checks instead
explanation: DNS failover is only as fast as the TTL because resolvers cache the answer. Lowering the TTL (e.g. 60 s) shortens the window during which clients keep using the failed primary.
distractors: Failover records can be plain A records; alias is not required.
A secondary without a health check is treated as healthy; it is not what delayed the switch.
Global Accelerator is a different service; the described lag is DNS caching, which health check interval alone does not fix.

stem: A company serves large static assets from S3 to users worldwide and pays significant data-transfer-out charges. It also deploys new asset versions daily and wants those to appear immediately without paying repeatedly to purge the cache. Which TWO actions are MOST cost-effective? (Choose TWO.)
options: Use versioned filenames for each release instead of invalidations
Enable Requester Pays on the bucket
Move the assets to S3 Express One Zone
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket with a long TTL
explanation: CloudFront egress is cheaper than S3-direct egress and cache hits never touch the origin. Versioned filenames (app.4f2a.js) make new releases visible instantly without invalidations, which cost at scale.
distractors: Requester Pays only shifts cost to AWS-authenticated requesters; anonymous website visitors cannot pay.
Express One Zone is a single-AZ low-latency class; it does not reduce internet egress and is not a CDN.
Transfer Acceleration is for uploads and adds a per-GB fee; it does not cut download egress.

stem: A video-on-demand platform stores thousands of files per course in a private S3 bucket. After a user buys a course, they must be able to stream any file in it globally for 24 hours, and the bucket must never be public. Which solution is MOST appropriate?
options: Generate an S3 presigned URL for each file when the video player requests it from the API
CloudFront with Origin Access Control and signed cookies scoped to the course path
A public bucket with a bucket policy that limits reads to the purchasing user's IP address
CloudFront with geo restriction enabled for the country the buyer registered from
explanation: OAC keeps the bucket private and readable only by CloudFront; signed cookies grant time-limited access to many files at once (a whole course), served from the edge with caching.
distractors: Presigned URLs are per object, served from the bucket's Region with no CDN, and would need a new URL for every file.
Public bucket violates the requirement and IP restriction fails for mobile users.
Geo restriction filters by country; it does not authorise individual buyers.

stem: An e-commerce site behind CloudFront uses an ALB in eu-west-1 as its origin. The company wants CloudFront to automatically serve from a second ALB in eu-central-1 if the primary origin returns 5xx errors, with no DNS changes. What should be configured?
options: A Lambda@Edge function that rewrites the origin when the primary returns an error
A Route 53 failover record for the origin's domain name with a health check on each ALB
A CloudFront origin group with the primary and secondary origins
A second CloudFront distribution pointing at the secondary ALB with a shared alias
explanation: Origin groups give CloudFront origin-level failover: on configured error codes from the primary, it retries the request against the secondary origin, without any DNS involvement.
distractors: Custom edge code could do this but is far more to build and maintain than the native feature.
DNS failover is subject to TTL and does not react per request; origin groups are the built-in mechanism.
A separate distribution has a different domain name and does not fail over automatically.

stem: A financial trading platform uses a proprietary TCP protocol (not HTTP) served by NLBs in two Regions. Clients' firewalls only allow a fixed list of IP addresses, and failover between Regions must complete in seconds. Which service meets ALL requirements?
options: An Application Load Balancer in each Region with cross-zone load balancing enabled
Amazon CloudFront with the two NLBs configured as an origin group
Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks on each Regional NLB
AWS Global Accelerator with the two NLBs as endpoints
explanation: Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPs (easy to allow-list), supports any TCP or UDP protocol, and fails over between Regional endpoints at the network layer in seconds without DNS TTLs.
distractors: ALBs are HTTP layer 7 and Regional; they neither speak the custom TCP protocol nor fail over across Regions.
CloudFront is HTTP/HTTPS only and its addresses are a DNS name, not fixed IPs.
Route 53 returns changing IPs and failover waits for TTL expiry, so neither the fixed-IP nor the seconds-fast requirement is met.

stem: An application on Aurora MySQL has three replicas, but developers have hardcoded one replica's instance endpoint for read traffic and that instance is saturated while the others sit idle. What is the SIMPLEST change to spread reads evenly?
options: Add a Network Load Balancer in front of the three replica instances
Point read traffic at the cluster's reader endpoint
Enable Aurora Multi-master so every instance can serve reads
Create a custom endpoint containing only the saturated instance
explanation: The reader endpoint is a built-in DNS name that load-balances connections across all Aurora replicas in the cluster and adjusts automatically as replicas are added, removed or fail over. No extra infrastructure is needed.
distractors: A load balancer works but adds infrastructure and cost for something Aurora already provides via the reader endpoint.
Multi-master is about multiple writers in one Region and is a niche feature; the replicas already serve reads — the problem is how traffic reaches them.
A custom endpoint targets a named subset of instances; one containing only the busy instance changes nothing.

stem: A single-AZ RDS PostgreSQL instance causes several minutes of application downtime every time AWS applies an engine minor-version patch or the team changes the instance class. Downtime from these events must be minimised without changing the application. What should the solutions architect do?
options: Add a read replica and promote it before every maintenance event
Enable storage autoscaling on the instance
Convert the instance to a Multi-AZ deployment
Schedule the maintenance window during off-peak hours
explanation: Multi-AZ applies patches and instance-class changes to the standby first, then fails over (typically 60–120 s) and repeats on the old primary. Because the DNS endpoint stays the same, the application reconnects instead of being reconfigured, so maintenance downtime drops from minutes to a brief failover.
distractors: Promoting a replica creates a separate standalone instance with a new endpoint; it is a manual DR step, not a maintenance-downtime feature.
Storage autoscaling grows the volume when it fills; it has nothing to do with patching or instance-class changes.
Off-peak scheduling reduces impact but the downtime still happens; the requirement is to minimise it.
