stem: A B2B SaaS product uses Aurora PostgreSQL. Its load is near zero overnight and at weekends but spikes unpredictably by 20× when large customers run imports, and the provisioned r6g.4xlarge writer is idle most of the time. Which change is MOST cost-effective while still absorbing the spikes?
options: Move to Aurora Serverless v2 with a minimum and maximum ACU range
Downsize the writer to r6g.large and add three read replicas for the imports
Buy a three-year Reserved Instance for the r6g.4xlarge writer instance
Replace Aurora with DynamoDB on-demand and rewrite the import path
explanation: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity (ACUs) up and down in fine increments within seconds and shrinks to the minimum when idle, so you pay for the overnight lull at the floor and for the spikes only while they happen — the intended answer for intermittent or spiky relational load.
distractors: Import spikes are write-heavy; read replicas don't scale writes and a downsized writer would fall over during imports.
A Reserved Instance discounts capacity that is idle most of the time — cheaper per hour but still paying for 4xlarge around the clock.
Rewriting a relational SaaS schema for DynamoDB is a re-architecture, not a cost tuning, and nothing says the access patterns fit key-value.

stem: A deployment ran a faulty data migration against a production Aurora MySQL cluster 20 minutes ago and corrupted several tables. The team must return the cluster to its pre-migration state as QUICKLY as possible. What should they do?
options: Restore the latest automated snapshot to a new cluster and repoint the application
Use point-in-time recovery to create a new cluster from 25 minutes ago
Use Aurora Backtrack to rewind the existing cluster to a time before the migration
Fail over to an Aurora replica, which still holds the pre-migration data
explanation: Backtrack rewinds an Aurora cluster in place to a chosen point in time within the backtrack window, without creating a new cluster or changing endpoints — minutes rather than the tens of minutes a restore takes. It must have been enabled on the cluster.
distractors: A snapshot restore creates a new cluster with a new endpoint and can take a long time for a large volume; it also loses everything since the last snapshot.
PITR also produces a new cluster that must be repointed and warmed; correct in principle but slower than Backtrack.
Aurora replicas read the same shared storage volume as the writer, so they hold the same corrupted data.

stem: A compliance team requires that an application on EC2 connect to RDS MySQL without any long-lived database password stored on the instances or in configuration files. Which approach meets the requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Store the password in an encrypted S3 object and fetch it at start-up with the instance role
Use RDS Proxy with a static password configured in the proxy and connect through the proxy
Bake the password into the AMI and rotate the AMI monthly with EC2 Image Builder
Enable IAM database authentication and have the instance role generate authentication tokens
explanation: IAM database authentication lets the instance role request a short-lived (15-minute) authentication token from RDS instead of presenting a password. Nothing long-lived is stored anywhere and access is governed by IAM policy.
distractors: An encrypted object is still a long-lived password that must be rotated and protected — the requirement was to have none.
RDS Proxy can enforce IAM auth, but configured with a static password it still relies on a stored secret.
An AMI-embedded password is the worst form of long-lived credential; it travels with every copy of the image.

stem: A company runs RDS for PostgreSQL in eu-west-1 with Multi-AZ enabled. A new policy says the database must survive the loss of the entire Region with an RPO of a few minutes and an RTO under an hour, using the fewest changes to the existing setup. What should the architect add?
options: A second Multi-AZ standby in eu-central-1, promoted automatically during a Regional outage
A cross-Region read replica in eu-central-1 that can be promoted during a Regional outage
A nightly automated snapshot copy to eu-central-1 restored to a new instance on failover
An Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in eu-central-1 for fast failover
explanation: A cross-Region read replica replicates asynchronously — typically seconds to minutes behind — and can be promoted to a standalone instance in another Region, giving an RPO of minutes and an RTO well under an hour without changing the engine or the application.
distractors: Multi-AZ standbys live in another AZ of the same Region; RDS has no cross-Region standby.
A nightly copy gives an RPO of up to 24 hours, far outside the requirement.
Aurora Global Database is the best multi-Region answer, but it requires migrating from RDS PostgreSQL to Aurora — not the fewest changes.

stem: A legacy Oracle application relies on custom OS-level agents and file-system access on the database host, but the company wants AWS to handle backups, patching and monitoring as far as possible. Which database platform should they choose?
options: Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with the Babelfish extension
Amazon RDS for Oracle
Amazon DocumentDB
explanation: RDS Custom keeps most of RDS's managed operations while granting OS and database access to the underlying host — built exactly for legacy Oracle and SQL Server applications that need customisation standard RDS forbids.
distractors: Babelfish targets SQL Server T-SQL, not Oracle, and Aurora offers no OS access at all.
Standard RDS gives no host access; you cannot install OS agents or touch the file system.
DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible; it does not run Oracle workloads.

stem: An RDS MySQL instance backs a web application. Two new requirements arrive: the database must keep serving traffic through an AZ failure without manual action, and the read load from an analytics dashboard must stop competing with application queries. Which TWO changes meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
options: Enable Multi-AZ on the instance
Create one or more read replicas and point the dashboard at them
Place RDS Proxy in front of the instance
Enable storage autoscaling on the instance
Schedule a daily snapshot copy to another Region
explanation: Multi-AZ gives synchronous replication and automatic failover for the availability requirement; read replicas give asynchronous, readable copies for the read-scaling requirement. They compose — one instance can have both.
distractors: RDS Proxy pools connections and shortens failover but doesn't survive an AZ loss on its own or serve reads.
Storage autoscaling grows the disk; it addresses neither availability nor read load.
A cross-Region snapshot copy is a DR measure with hours of RPO and manual restore, not automatic AZ failover.

stem: A document-management application stores metadata in DynamoDB and now needs to keep the documents themselves, typically 2–5 MB each, alongside the metadata. Writes to DynamoDB fail for these records. What should the architect do?
options: Compress the documents so that each one fits into a single DynamoDB item
Store the documents in Amazon S3 and keep the object key in the DynamoDB item
Split each document across multiple items that share the same partition key
Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode to allow larger items to be written
explanation: DynamoDB items are capped at 400 KB. The standard pattern for larger payloads is to store the blob in S3 and keep a pointer (bucket and key) plus metadata in the table.
distractors: Compression cannot reliably bring multi-megabyte documents under the 400 KB item limit.
Splitting blobs across items works around the limit but adds reassembly logic and multiplies write cost; S3 is the intended store for objects.
Capacity mode governs throughput billing, not item size.

stem: An e-commerce team is designing a DynamoDB table so the app can retrieve all orders for a given customer, most recent first, in one efficient call. Orders are also looked up individually. Which key design supports this?
options: Partition key orderId; use a Scan with a filter expression on customerId and sort client-side
Partition key orderTimestamp and sort key customerId; use Query on the timestamp range
Partition key customerId and sort key orderTimestamp; use Query with ScanIndexForward=false
A single partition key customerId with all of the customer's orders stored in one list attribute
explanation: Items sharing a partition key are stored together ordered by sort key, so Query on customerId returns that customer's orders already ordered by timestamp, and reversing the sort is a flag. Individual orders are fetched with the full key.
distractors: Scan reads the entire table and filters afterwards — slow, expensive and the wrong answer whenever a Query would do.
Partitioning by timestamp means a customer's orders are scattered across partitions and Query cannot fetch them together; it also creates a hot partition on the current time.
One item cannot exceed 400 KB and would be rewritten wholesale on every order — no scaling and no per-order lookup.

stem: A start-up is launching a mobile game backed by DynamoDB. Traffic could be tens of requests per second or tens of thousands depending on whether the game goes viral, and the team has no historical data. Which capacity mode is the MOST cost-effective choice at launch?
options: Provisioned capacity sized for the optimistic forecast
Provisioned capacity with reserved capacity purchased for three years
On-demand capacity
Provisioned capacity with auto scaling and a very high maximum
explanation: On-demand bills per request and scales instantly with no forecast required — the intended answer for new, unpredictable or spiky workloads. Once traffic settles into a pattern, provisioned becomes cheaper.
distractors: Sizing for an optimistic forecast pays for capacity that may never be used, or throttles if the guess is low.
Reserved capacity locks in spend for a workload whose size is completely unknown.
Auto scaling reacts to observed load with a lag and still bills the provisioned floor; it suits predictable patterns, not a launch with no data.

stem: A DynamoDB table on on-demand mode serves an internal HR portal. CloudWatch shows a very regular pattern: about 500 reads per second during office hours and near zero at night, every weekday for the past year. The finance team asks for savings. What should the architect recommend?
options: Keep on-demand mode and enable DAX so that fewer reads reach the table
Enable a global table so that reads are spread across two Regions and each Region is billed at a lower rate
Switch to provisioned capacity fixed at the office-hours peak for reads and writes
Switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling between a low minimum and a peak-sized maximum
explanation: Provisioned capacity is considerably cheaper per unit than on-demand for steady, predictable traffic, and auto scaling follows the daily curve within the min/max band so you are not paying peak rates overnight. Reserved capacity can cut it further.
distractors: DAX cuts read latency and can absorb repeated reads, but it adds cluster cost and doesn't change the fact that on-demand is the expensive mode for a predictable load.
Global Tables add replica Regions and cost; they solve multi-Region latency, not billing.
Fixed peak capacity pays for 500 RCU all night for nothing; auto scaling avoids that.

stem: After a team added a global secondary index to a busy provisioned-capacity DynamoDB table, application writes to the base table began returning ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, although the table's own write capacity has not changed and its consumed WCU is under the limit. What is the cause?
options: The GSI is eventually consistent, so writes must wait for the index to catch up before they succeed
The GSI's provisioned write capacity is lower than the write rate it must absorb
Adding a GSI halves the base table's available write capacity until the index is backfilled
The table's partition key became a hot partition when the index was created and backfilled
explanation: A GSI has its own RCU/WCU. Every base-table write also writes the index entry, so if the GSI is under-provisioned for the write rate, DynamoDB throttles the base-table write. "Writes started failing after we added an index" is this trap every time.
distractors: Eventual consistency describes reads from a GSI; it does not block writes.
A GSI does not consume the table's capacity — that is an LSI's behaviour, and even then it shares rather than halves.
Creating an index does not change the base table's key distribution; nothing in the scenario points to a low-cardinality key.

stem: A team is designing a new DynamoDB table for support tickets keyed by customerId (partition) and ticketId (sort). They also need to fetch a customer's tickets ordered by priority, and those reads must be strongly consistent because agents act on them immediately. What should the design include?
options: A global secondary index with customerId as partition key and priority as sort key
A second table keyed by priority, kept in sync with DynamoDB Streams
A local secondary index with priority as the sort key, defined when the table is created
A global secondary index with priority as partition key, queried with ConsistentRead=true
explanation: An LSI keeps the table's partition key and adds an alternative sort key, can be read with strong consistency, and — the deciding constraint — can only be created at table creation time, which is exactly the situation here.
distractors: A GSI can only be read eventually consistently, so it fails the strong-consistency requirement.
A Streams-fed copy is eventually consistent by nature and adds moving parts an LSI makes unnecessary.
GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads regardless of the parameter, and priority as a partition key would concentrate traffic on a few values.

stem: A mobile app authenticates users through Amazon Cognito and stores each user's data in a single DynamoDB table with userId as the partition key. Users must be able to read and write only their own items, using credentials issued to the app. How should this be enforced?
options: Create a separate DynamoDB table per user and grant each Cognito identity access to its own table through IAM
Attach an IAM policy to the Cognito identity role with a dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition on the identity id
Encrypt each user's items with a per-user KMS key whose key policy names that user's identity
Put an API Gateway in front of DynamoDB and filter the results by userId in a Lambda authorizer
explanation: DynamoDB fine-grained access control uses the IAM condition dynamodb:LeadingKeys, so the policy allows only items whose partition key equals the caller's Cognito identity — enforced by the service, not by the client.
distractors: A table per user does not scale and defeats DynamoDB's single-table access patterns.
Encryption controls confidentiality at rest, not which rows an authenticated user may read or write.
A middle tier can work but is heavier than a native IAM condition and the question asks for direct app credentials.

stem: A web application stores user session records in DynamoDB. Sessions become useless 24 hours after creation, but the table keeps growing and storage costs climb. What is the MOST cost-effective way to remove expired sessions?
options: Run a nightly Lambda function that scans the table and deletes the expired items
Enable point-in-time recovery and periodically restore a smaller table from it
Switch the table to on-demand capacity so that unused items cost less to store
Enable Time to Live on a timestamp attribute holding the session expiry
explanation: TTL deletes items asynchronously once the timestamp attribute passes, and the deletions consume no write capacity — free housekeeping with no code to run.
distractors: A Scan-and-delete job consumes read and write capacity every night and is exactly what TTL replaces.
PITR is a backup feature; restoring does not remove data and creates a new table.
Capacity mode changes throughput billing; storage is billed by size in either mode.

stem: A product catalogue lives in DynamoDB. The company adds Amazon OpenSearch Service for full-text search and needs every insert, update and delete in the table to be reflected in the search index within seconds, without changing the application code that writes to the table. What should the architect implement?
options: Enable DynamoDB Streams and trigger a Lambda function that writes each change to OpenSearch
Schedule an hourly Lambda function that scans the table and reindexes everything in OpenSearch
Enable global tables with the OpenSearch domain configured as an additional replica Region
Modify the application to write to DynamoDB and to OpenSearch in the same transaction
explanation: DynamoDB Streams emits an ordered log of every item change; a Lambda trigger consumes it and updates OpenSearch in near real time. The writing application is untouched.
distractors: An hourly full Scan is expensive and violates the seconds-level freshness requirement.
Global Tables replicate between DynamoDB Regions only; OpenSearch is not a replica target.
Dual-writing changes the application code and creates consistency problems when one write fails.

stem: An online retailer stores shopping carts in DynamoDB. During sales, reads of a few hot product records dominate and must return in microseconds without rewriting the application, and abandoned carts must disappear automatically after 30 days. Which TWO features address these needs? (Choose TWO.)
options: ElastiCache for Memcached with cache-aside logic in the application
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table
DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda that deletes old carts
Time to Live on an expiry attribute of each cart item
Global Tables in a second Region
explanation: DAX is DynamoDB's own in-memory, write-through cache that the SDK talks to transparently, delivering microsecond reads for hot items with no application logic change. TTL expires the abandoned carts for free.
distractors: ElastiCache would work but requires writing and maintaining cache-aside code — the question rules out an application rewrite.
Streams react to changes; deleting old items would still need scheduled logic and write capacity, which TTL avoids.
Global Tables solve multi-Region latency, not hot-key read latency or expiry.

stem: A multiplayer game needs a real-time leaderboard ranked by score, plus a pub/sub channel to push updates to connected players. The cache must survive a node failure without losing the leaderboard. Which service fits?
options: ElastiCache for Memcached with multiple nodes in several AZs
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of a leaderboard table
ElastiCache for Redis with replication and Multi-AZ
Amazon MQ with a RabbitMQ broker and a topic per match
explanation: Sorted sets, pub/sub, persistence and replica-based automatic failover are Redis capabilities; Memcached offers none of them. Leaderboards are the textbook Redis scenario.
distractors: Memcached stores plain key-value strings, has no sorted sets or pub/sub, and its nodes are independent — a failed node's data is gone.
DAX only accelerates DynamoDB reads; it offers no data structures or messaging.
Amazon MQ is a message broker for JMS/AMQP migrations, not a ranked in-memory store.

stem: A web tier caches rendered HTML fragments that can be regenerated at any time. The team wants the cheapest, simplest cache that scales horizontally by adding nodes and can use multiple CPU cores per node; losing the cache on failure is acceptable. Which option is MOST appropriate?
options: ElastiCache for Memcached
ElastiCache for Redis with AOF persistence enabled
ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode with Multi-AZ
DynamoDB with DAX
explanation: Memcached is the simple, multi-threaded, horizontally sharded object cache for disposable data. When persistence, replication and rich data types are explicitly not needed, it is the cheaper and simpler pick.
distractors: AOF persistence protects data the scenario says is disposable.
Cluster mode with Multi-AZ buys HA and sharding you were told you don't need, at higher cost.
Introducing a database plus its cache for throwaway HTML fragments is heavier than a plain cache.

stem: A media site backs a catalogue of millions of articles with a relational database, but readers request only a small, shifting subset each day. The team adds ElastiCache and wants to keep memory usage low while accepting slightly stale content for a few minutes. Which caching strategy should they use?
options: Write-through: update the cache on every article write with no TTL
Lazy loading (cache-aside) with a TTL on each cached article
Write-through with a TTL on each article that matches the publishing cadence
Pre-warm the whole catalogue into the cache every night with a batch job
explanation: Cache-aside populates the cache only on a read miss, so memory holds just the articles that are actually requested; a TTL bounds how stale an entry can be. Write-through would push every article into memory whether or not anyone reads it.
distractors: Write-through caches everything written, including the millions of articles nobody reads — high memory use.
Same memory problem, and without a TTL entries never expire.
Loading the whole catalogue defeats the goal of low memory usage.

stem: A company is moving a self-managed Apache Kafka estate to AWS. Dozens of producers and consumers use the Kafka client libraries and must move without code changes, but the team wants to stop patching and scaling brokers themselves. Which service should they use?
options: Amazon MSK (Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka)
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with the Kinesis Client Library
Amazon SQS FIFO queues with message group IDs per topic
Amazon Data Firehose delivering to an S3 bucket
explanation: MSK runs real Apache Kafka clusters as a managed service, so existing Kafka clients connect unchanged while AWS handles broker provisioning, patching and scaling. The word "Kafka" in a migration scenario is the cue.
distractors: Kinesis Data Streams is a similar streaming log but uses its own API; Kafka clients would need rewriting.
SQS FIFO is a work queue with no Kafka compatibility, replay or multi-consumer semantics.
Firehose is a delivery pipe to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch, not a Kafka-compatible broker.

stem: Sensor readings arrive in a Kinesis data stream. Operations staff need a dashboard of the average temperature per site over a sliding five-minute window, updated continuously, and an alert when it exceeds a threshold. Which service should compute the windowed aggregates?
options: Amazon Athena querying the stream through a Glue table on a schedule
AWS Glue ETL jobs on a five-minute schedule writing to a dashboard table
Amazon Data Firehose with a Lambda transformation computing the average
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink consuming the stream
explanation: Managed Service for Apache Flink runs SQL or Flink applications directly over a stream and is built for continuous, windowed aggregations in real time. "Analyse the stream in real time" is its cue.
distractors: Athena queries data at rest in S3; it does not consume a live stream.
Glue is batch ETL; a scheduled job is not continuous, sub-minute analysis.
Firehose's Lambda transform operates record by record during delivery; it has no state for sliding-window aggregation.

stem: A payments team ingests transaction events into AWS. A bug in a downstream consumer silently dropped events for three days, and the team wants to reprocess those events from the ingestion layer once the fix ships. Which ingestion service would have made this possible?
options: Amazon Data Firehose delivering to S3 with the maximum buffer interval of 900 seconds
Amazon SNS with a Lambda subscriber and a retry policy of three days
Amazon SQS standard queue with the maximum message retention of 14 days
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with retention extended beyond the default 24 hours
explanation: Kinesis Data Streams retains records for 1–365 days and lets any consumer re-read from an earlier position, so a fixed consumer can replay the missed window. Firehose keeps nothing once delivered.
distractors: Firehose delivers and forgets; you could reprocess from S3 only if the *destination* still holds the data, and the question asks about the ingestion layer.
SNS pushes and does not store messages; a failed subscriber cannot go back three days.
SQS deletes messages once a consumer processes them; there is no replay of consumed messages.

stem: An image-processing service receives unpredictable bursts of upload jobs. Each job must be processed by exactly one worker in a fleet, order does not matter, and there is no need to reprocess jobs later. Which service should sit between the uploader and the workers?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon SQS standard queue
explanation: This is a work queue: one consumer group, each message deleted after processing, no ordering or replay requirement. SQS is the decouple-and-process-once answer; Kinesis is for ordered, replayable, multi-consumer logs.
distractors: Kinesis Data Streams gives ordering, retention and multiple consumers you don't need, and shard management on top.
Firehose delivers data to storage destinations; it does not dispatch jobs to a worker fleet.
Flink analyses streams; it is not a job-distribution mechanism.

stem: Clickstream data lands in S3 via Data Firehose as partitioned Parquet files. The company wants analysts to run ad-hoc SQL over it and business users to build dashboards, with NO clusters to manage and pay-per-use pricing. Which TWO services complete the design? (Choose TWO.)
options: A Glue crawler to populate the Data Catalog, queried by Athena
A provisioned Amazon Redshift cluster loaded nightly with COPY
Amazon QuickSight for the dashboards
An EMR cluster running Presto
AWS Data Exchange
explanation: Athena runs serverless SQL directly over S3 using table definitions the Glue crawler discovers, billed per TB scanned; QuickSight is serverless BI on top of it. No clusters, pay per use, and Parquet plus partitioning keeps the scan bill down.
distractors: A provisioned Redshift cluster is a running warehouse to size and pay for around the clock — the opposite of no clusters.
EMR means managing a Hadoop/Presto cluster; the requirement rules that out.
Data Exchange is for subscribing to third-party datasets, not querying your own.

stem: A nightly batch job on EC2 must alert the operations team by email and SMS the moment it fails, with the least custom code. Which service should the job publish its failure notification to?
options: An SQS queue that the operations team polls
An SNS topic with email and SMS subscriptions
An EventBridge rule targeting a Lambda function that sends emails
A Kinesis data stream consumed by a notification service
explanation: SNS is push-based publish/subscribe with native email, SMS and mobile push subscribers. One publish call notifies everyone; no consumer code is needed.
distractors: SQS is pull-based and holds messages for a consumer; people do not poll queues, and it has no email/SMS delivery.
EventBridge can route the event, but writing a Lambda to send email is custom code that SNS makes unnecessary.
Kinesis is a streaming log for high-volume data, not an alerting channel.

stem: A worker fleet polls an SQS queue in a tight loop. Most ReceiveMessage calls return nothing because the queue is empty most of the time, and the SQS bill is dominated by these empty requests. What is the MOST cost-effective fix?
options: Increase the visibility timeout so that messages are redelivered less frequently
Convert the queue to a FIFO queue so that empty receives are not billed
Enable long polling by setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds
Add a dead-letter queue so that empty responses are absorbed and not billed
explanation: Long polling makes ReceiveMessage wait up to 20 seconds for a message to arrive before returning, which eliminates most empty responses — fewer billed requests and lower latency when a message does arrive.
distractors: Visibility timeout affects how long a received message is hidden; it has nothing to do with empty polls.
FIFO changes ordering and de-duplication semantics; empty polls are billed the same way.
A DLQ collects messages that fail processing repeatedly; it does not change polling behaviour.

stem: A pipeline sends job requests through SQS. A new job type carries a 2 MB payload and SendMessage rejects it. What is the recommended way to keep using SQS for these jobs?
options: Switch to a FIFO queue, which supports messages larger than 256 KB
Use the SQS Extended Client Library so the payload is stored in S3 and the message carries a pointer
Compress the payload with gzip so that it fits under the 256 KB message size limit
Split each job into eight 256 KB messages, send them as a batch, and reassemble the payload on the consumer
explanation: SQS messages are limited to 256 KB. The Extended Client Library transparently stores large payloads in an S3 bucket and sends a reference in the message; the consumer library fetches it back.
distractors: FIFO queues have the same 256 KB limit as standard queues.
Compression may not reliably bring 2 MB under 256 KB and makes size unpredictable.
Manual splitting adds ordering and reassembly complexity that the Extended Client Library avoids.

stem: An Auto Scaling group of workers consumes an SQS queue and scales on average CPU utilisation. During bursts the queue backlog grows for a long time before extra workers appear, because CPU stays moderate while each worker waits on downstream calls. What should the architect change?
options: Scale on the queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, ideally as backlog per instance
Lower the CPU threshold of the scaling policy to 20% so that scale-out starts earlier
Increase the visibility timeout so messages stay hidden while the existing workers catch up
Enable long polling on the workers so that each ReceiveMessage call returns more messages
explanation: The right signal for a queue-driven fleet is queue depth, not CPU. Scaling on ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible (per instance) adds workers as soon as backlog builds regardless of how busy each worker's CPU looks.
distractors: A lower CPU threshold still measures the wrong thing; I/O-bound workers may never cross it while the backlog explodes.
Hiding messages longer changes nothing about how quickly the backlog is drained.
Long polling reduces empty receives; it does not add processing capacity.

stem: An order service publishes every order event to one SNS topic. The refunds team only wants events whose type is REFUND, the shipping team only SHIPPED, and each team consumes through its own SQS queue. How should this be implemented with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a separate SNS topic per event type and have the publisher choose the topic for each event
Replace SNS with an SQS FIFO queue and use the message group ID to carry the event type
Have each team's consumer receive every message and discard those of other event types
Apply an SNS subscription filter policy on each queue's subscription matching the event type
explanation: SNS message filtering lets each subscription declare a filter policy on message attributes, so each queue receives only the messages it cares about while the publisher keeps publishing to a single topic.
distractors: Multiple topics work but push routing logic into the publisher and multiply topics as event types grow.
A single SQS queue cannot fan out one message to several independent consumers; message groups are for ordering, not routing.
Delivering everything to everyone wastes queue throughput and consumer time — filtering at the subscription is free.

stem: A company wants Zendesk ticket events to trigger workflows in AWS, route them to different Lambda functions based on ticket priority in the event body, and be able to replay the last week of events after fixing a consumer bug. Which service should be the backbone?
options: Amazon SNS with subscription filter policies and a Lambda subscriber per priority
Amazon EventBridge with a partner event source, content-based rules and an event archive
Amazon SQS FIFO with a dispatcher Lambda function that routes each message on the ticket priority
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams fed by a custom Zendesk poller running on a schedule
explanation: EventBridge natively ingests partner SaaS events (Zendesk among them), routes on any JSON field with rules, and its archive-and-replay feature re-emits past events — all three requirements without custom integration code.
distractors: SNS filters on message attributes and has no SaaS partner sources or replay.
SQS FIFO has no content routing and no replay after processing; a dispatcher Lambda is custom code EventBridge rules replace.
Kinesis provides replay but you would have to build the Zendesk integration and the routing logic yourself.

stem: An expense-approval workflow runs several Lambda steps, then pauses until a manager approves — which can take up to three business days — before continuing. Each approval must run exactly once and the team wants full execution history. Which Step Functions configuration fits?
options: A Standard workflow
An Express workflow with a Wait state
Two Express workflows chained by an SQS queue
A single long-running Lambda function that polls for approval
explanation: Standard workflows run for up to a year with exactly-once execution semantics and full execution history — built for long-lived processes with human approval steps. Express workflows cap at five minutes and are at-least-once.
distractors: Express workflows cannot run longer than five minutes, so a multi-day wait is impossible.
Chaining two Express workflows still leaves nothing to hold the multi-day wait state, and Express is at-least-once.
Lambda invocations cap at 15 minutes and polling for days is a mis-use of compute.

stem: An on-premises order system exchanges messages over AMQP with several downstream applications using RabbitMQ. The company is migrating to AWS and cannot rewrite the messaging code in the short term. Which service should host the broker?
options: Amazon MQ
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon SQS
Amazon EventBridge
explanation: Amazon MQ is managed ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ that speaks standard protocols — AMQP, JMS, MQTT, STOMP, OpenWire — so applications migrate without changing their messaging code. That is its one exam purpose.
distractors: Kinesis is a streaming log with its own API, not an AMQP broker.
SQS has its own API; the AMQP clients would have to be rewritten.
EventBridge is an event bus with an AWS API; it does not speak AMQP.

stem: A video platform's web tier hands transcoding jobs to a fleet of workers. Jobs must never be lost, spikes must be absorbed, order does not matter, and occasional corrupt uploads that always fail must not block the other jobs. Which TWO components should the design include? (Choose TWO.)
options: An SNS topic invoking the workers directly
An SQS standard queue between the web tier and the workers
A dead-letter queue with a maxReceiveCount on the main queue
An SQS FIFO queue between the web tier and the workers
An EventBridge Scheduler rule that retries failed jobs hourly
explanation: A standard queue durably buffers jobs and absorbs spikes for a worker fleet that doesn't need ordering; a DLQ moves messages that repeatedly fail aside after maxReceiveCount so poison jobs stop clogging the queue.
distractors: SNS pushes with no durable buffer per consumer — if workers are down or overwhelmed, jobs are lost or throttled.
FIFO adds ordering and throughput limits the workload doesn't need; standard is the default when order doesn't matter.
A schedule cannot know which jobs failed; the DLQ pattern handles poison messages.

stem: Regulators require that a record of every management API call in the AWS account be retained for seven years and be provably unaltered. What should the solutions architect configure?
options: Rely on CloudTrail Event History in the console, which retains management events indefinitely at no cost
Enable AWS Config to record every API call and set a seven-year retention on its recorder
Create a trail delivering to S3 with log file validation enabled and Object Lock on the bucket
Stream CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs and set a seven-year retention on the log group
explanation: Event History keeps only 90 days. A trail into S3 gives unlimited retention; log file validation produces digests that prove files were not modified, and Object Lock makes the bucket write-once — the standard tamper-evident audit answer.
distractors: Event History is limited to 90 days of management events.
Config records resource configuration changes, not API call history.
CloudWatch Logs can hold the events, but it offers no cryptographic integrity guarantee like log file validation plus Object Lock.

stem: An Auto Scaling group scales on average CPU, but during sudden traffic spikes new instances arrive minutes too late. Metrics for the instances are only published every five minutes. What should the architect change to make scaling react faster?
options: Install the CloudWatch agent on the instances and publish CPU as a one-minute custom metric
Switch the alarm's missing-data handling to treat missing data points as breaching the threshold
Create a composite alarm that combines the CPU metric with the network metrics for the group
Enable detailed monitoring on the instances so metrics are published at one-minute granularity
explanation: Basic EC2 monitoring publishes at 5-minute intervals; detailed monitoring (chargeable) publishes at 1 minute, so alarms and scaling policies see the spike far sooner.
distractors: The agent adds guest-level metrics such as memory and disk; CPU is already reported by the hypervisor, and the fix here is granularity.
Missing-data treatment governs alarm behaviour on gaps, not metric frequency.
A composite alarm reduces noise; it does not make the underlying data arrive faster.

stem: A stateful EC2 instance with an Elastic IP occasionally fails its system status check due to underlying host problems. The team wants it brought back automatically on healthy hardware with the same instance ID and IP, without a human intervening. What should they configure?
options: An Auto Scaling group of size 1 with a health check that replaces the instance
A CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the EC2 recover action
An EventBridge rule on instance state change that reboots the instance
A Lambda function scheduled to ping the instance every minute and restart it
explanation: CloudWatch alarms can take EC2 actions — stop, terminate, reboot or recover. Recover migrates the instance to new hardware keeping its instance ID, private IP, Elastic IP and metadata, exactly matching a system-level failure.
distractors: An ASG replaces the instance with a new one — new instance ID and, unless scripted, a new IP; not what was asked.
A reboot on the same failed host may not help, and state-change events fire after the fact rather than on a failed status check.
Custom polling reinvents a built-in alarm action and a restart doesn't move the instance off bad hardware.

stem: Developers need to run database tools on their laptops against an RDS instance in a private subnet. The security team forbids bastion hosts, public database endpoints, and inbound SSH anywhere in the VPC, and requires every connection to be tied to an IAM identity. Which approach satisfies this?
options: A bastion host in a public subnet with a tightly scoped security group and session recording
A Site-to-Site VPN from the corporate network with the database security group opened to the VPN range
EC2 Instance Connect to a jump instance over the public internet with an ephemeral key per session
AWS Systems Manager Session Manager port forwarding through an SSM-managed instance
explanation: Session Manager can forward a local port to a remote host reachable from a managed instance, so a developer's laptop connects to the private RDS endpoint through the SSM channel. No inbound ports, keys or bastion are needed, the session is authorised by IAM and can be logged.
distractors: A bastion is explicitly excluded, and it still needs port 22 open somewhere.
A VPN gives network reachability but ties access to a network path, not to an IAM identity, and requires the database to accept the whole VPN range.
EC2 Instance Connect still uses SSH on port 22 and a jump instance, both of which the security team forbids.

stem: A team wants a central, versioned place for application configuration values such as feature flags and endpoint URLs, plus a few database connection strings that must be encrypted. The credentials are rotated manually once a year and cost must be minimal. Which service fits?
options: AWS Secrets Manager for every value, with automatic rotation disabled on each of the secrets
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with SecureString parameters for the sensitive values
AWS Config with a custom configuration item per value and encryption enabled
AWS AppConfig with an S3 configuration store, with the secrets encrypted with SSE-KMS
explanation: Parameter Store's standard tier is free, stores plain and SecureString (KMS-encrypted) values, and versions them. Automatic rotation is the only thing it lacks, and the question rules that out.
distractors: Secrets Manager charges per secret and its differentiator — automatic rotation — isn't required here.
Config records resource configuration and compliance; it is not a config-value store.
AppConfig manages deployment of configuration; storing secrets in S3 is not the fit and adds cost and moving parts.

stem: A company new to AWS must set up a secure multi-account environment within weeks, with preventive guardrails, an automated way to create new accounts, and single sign-on for staff from its existing identity provider. Which TWO services should form the foundation? (Choose TWO.)
options: AWS Control Tower
AWS Service Catalog
AWS Trusted Advisor
CloudFormation StackSets alone
AWS IAM Identity Center
explanation: Control Tower builds a well-architected landing zone on top of Organizations with guardrails and an Account Factory; IAM Identity Center provides SSO across all accounts with permission sets backed by an external IdP.
distractors: Service Catalog offers a curated menu of approved products to launch; it does not create the landing zone or provide SSO.
Trusted Advisor is a checks and recommendations tool, not a foundation for account structure.
StackSets deploy stacks across accounts but do not create accounts, guardrails or SSO.

stem: A company copies EBS snapshots encrypted with a customer managed KMS key from eu-west-1 to us-east-1 for disaster recovery. An engineer wants the copies to remain encrypted with the exact same key ARN so existing key policies keep working. What is the CORRECT explanation of what happens?
options: The copy is re-encrypted with a KMS key that lives in us-east-1, because KMS keys are Regional resources
The copy keeps the source key, because snapshot copies preserve their original encryption context and key
The copy is decrypted in transit and stored unencrypted unless a destination key is specified explicitly
The copy fails, because encrypted snapshots cannot be copied across Regions without re-importing the key
explanation: KMS keys are Regional resources, so a cross-Region snapshot copy is re-encrypted with a key in the destination Region. If the same key material must exist in both Regions, the answer is a multi-Region key.
distractors: A single-Region key cannot be referenced from another Region; the copy must use a destination-Region key.
Encrypted snapshots stay encrypted; the copy is re-encrypted, never written in plaintext.
Cross-Region copies of encrypted snapshots are supported and are the standard DR mechanism.

stem: A startup stores about 200 application configuration values, such as feature flags and endpoint URLs, plus a handful of API keys that are rotated manually once a year. They want a central store with the LOWEST cost. Which service should they use?
options: AWS Secrets Manager for every value, with automatic rotation disabled on each secret
An encrypted DynamoDB table with a Lambda-based lookup API in front of it for the applications
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store standard tier, using SecureString for the API keys
AWS Certificate Manager with a private certificate authority storing the values as metadata
explanation: Parameter Store standard parameters are free and SecureString parameters are KMS-encrypted, which fits configuration values and secrets that do not need automatic rotation.
distractors: Secrets Manager charges per secret per month; its advantage is built-in rotation, which this workload does not need.
This works but is a custom store to build and operate when a free managed one exists.
ACM issues TLS certificates; it is not a configuration or secret store.

stem: A company hosts a website in eu-central-1 behind an ALB and fronts it with CloudFront under a custom domain. They requested a public ACM certificate in eu-central-1 and attached it to the ALB, but the certificate is not selectable in the CloudFront distribution. What should they do?
options: Export the certificate from ACM in eu-central-1 and import it into ACM in us-east-1 for the CloudFront distribution
Request a second public ACM certificate for the same domain in us-east-1 and attach that one to CloudFront
Move the ALB and the origin to us-east-1 so that both resources can share the same certificate
Replace the public ACM certificate with one issued by AWS Private Certificate Authority
explanation: CloudFront is a global service that only reads ACM certificates from us-east-1. The ALB keeps its Regional certificate; CloudFront needs its own certificate issued in us-east-1.
distractors: Exporting a public certificate is a chargeable extra step (and the exported key must then be handled by you); requesting a free second certificate directly in us-east-1 is the intended path.
The origin's Region is irrelevant to which certificate CloudFront can use.
Private CA certificates are for internal trust; a public website needs a publicly trusted certificate.

stem: An auditor requires that a company can prove which principals used the encryption key protecting an S3 bucket, can rotate the key on a schedule they define, and can disable it immediately if it is suspected compromised. Which encryption configuration meets this with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: SSE-S3 with default bucket encryption
SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key aws/s3
Client-side encryption with keys stored in Parameter Store
SSE-KMS with a customer managed KMS key
explanation: Only a customer managed key gives you the key policy, on-demand or scheduled rotation, the ability to disable or schedule deletion, and per-use CloudTrail records. AWS still runs the hardware, so overhead stays low.
distractors: SSE-S3 keys are fully managed by S3 with no key policy, no rotation control and no per-key audit trail.
The AWS managed key rotates yearly automatically and cannot be disabled or given a custom key policy.
Client-side encryption meets the control requirement but pushes rotation, auditing and key handling onto the application.

stem: A mobile app must let users register with email and password, enforce MFA, and then read and write only their own items in a DynamoDB table directly from the device without a backend. Which two components are required? (Choose TWO.)
options: IAM Identity Center with a permission set per user
A Cognito user pool for sign-up, sign-in and MFA
An IAM user per app user with long-lived access keys embedded in the app
A Cognito identity pool that exchanges the user's token for temporary credentials scoped by a role with a dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition
An API Gateway REST API with a Lambda authorizer in front of the table
explanation: The user pool is the directory that authenticates the user and issues tokens; the identity pool exchanges that token for temporary AWS credentials whose IAM policy limits access to items keyed by the caller's identity.
distractors: IAM Identity Center is for workforce access to AWS accounts, not for an application's end users.
Embedding long-lived keys in a mobile app is an anti-pattern and does not scale to public sign-up.
This works but adds a backend; the requirement was direct access from the device with no backend.

stem: During a customer audit, a company is asked to provide AWS's own SOC 2 and PCI DSS compliance reports covering the underlying infrastructure. Where should they obtain these documents?
options: AWS Artifact
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Security Hub
AWS Config conformance packs
explanation: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for downloading AWS's own compliance reports such as SOC and PCI attestations.
distractors: Audit Manager collects evidence about your usage of AWS for your audits; it does not publish AWS's own reports.
Security Hub aggregates security findings; it does not host compliance attestations.
Conformance packs evaluate your resources against rules; they are not AWS's third-party audit reports.

stem: A security team must restrict outbound internet traffic from EC2 instances in a VPC so that only an allow-list of domain names can be reached, and must inspect traffic with intrusion-prevention signatures. Which service meets these requirements?
options: AWS WAF attached to the NAT gateway with a rule group that allows only the listed domains
Network ACLs with deny rules for known-bad IP ranges and allow rules for the listed domains
Security groups with outbound rules limited to port 443 and the IP addresses of the listed domains
AWS Network Firewall deployed in the VPC with stateful domain-filtering and IPS rules
explanation: Network Firewall is the VPC-level stateful firewall that supports domain-name filtering and Suricata-compatible intrusion detection and prevention rules on traffic entering and leaving the VPC.
distractors: WAF inspects HTTP requests at CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync and Cognito; it cannot attach to a NAT Gateway or filter egress by domain.
NACLs filter by IP and port only, are stateless and have no domain awareness or IPS capability.
Security groups cannot filter by domain name and perform no payload inspection.

stem: GuardDuty has flagged an EC2 instance communicating with a known command-and-control server. The security team now needs to reconstruct the sequence of API calls, network connections and related resources leading up to the finding, with the LEAST manual log correlation. Which service should they use?
options: Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie
Amazon Detective
AWS CloudTrail Lake
explanation: Detective ingests CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings and builds a behaviour graph so an analyst can investigate the root cause and timeline of a finding without hand-correlating logs.
distractors: Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and network exposure; it does not investigate incidents.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3; it plays no part in incident investigation.
CloudTrail Lake lets you query API events but does not correlate them with network activity or findings into an investigation graph.

stem: A business states that its order-processing system must be back in service within 10 minutes of a Regional outage. Which objective is being described, and what does meeting it primarily require?
options: An RPO of 10 minutes, met by replicating the data to the recovery Region every few minutes
An RPO of 10 minutes, met by taking backups every 10 minutes and copying them cross-Region
An RTO of 10 minutes, met by having capacity already provisioned in the recovery Region
An RTO of 10 minutes, met by copying AMIs to the recovery Region and launching them on failover
explanation: "Back within X" is a Recovery Time Objective. A short RTO is bought with pre-provisioned, running capacity, because launching a stack from scratch takes longer than ten minutes.
distractors: RPO measures data loss, not downtime.
RPO measures data loss, not downtime.
Copying AMIs is a pilot-light preparation; launching from AMIs during an incident is unlikely to fit inside a 10-minute RTO.

stem: A retailer needs its web platform to fail over to a second Region with an RTO of a few minutes and an RPO of seconds. Management will not pay for full duplicate capacity but accepts a scaled-down environment running continuously. Which DR strategy fits?
options: Warm standby
Pilot light
Backup and restore
Multi-site active-active
explanation: Warm standby keeps a complete but scaled-down stack running in the second Region, so failover is a scale-up rather than a launch, giving an RTO of minutes without paying for full production capacity.
distractors: Pilot light replicates data only; compute must be launched during failover, which typically means tens of minutes of RTO.
Backup and restore has an RTO of hours because everything is rebuilt from backups.
Active-active meets the objectives but requires full capacity in both Regions, which management has ruled out.

stem: An internal reporting application can tolerate up to 24 hours of data loss and up to 8 hours of downtime if its Region fails. Which cross-Region DR approach is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Aurora Global Database with a scaled-down application tier running in the second Region
A cross-Region read replica plus a running standby ALB and Auto Scaling group in the second Region
DynamoDB global tables with active-active Route 53 latency-based routing between the two Regions
Daily automated snapshots copied to the second Region, with the stack rebuilt from CloudFormation
explanation: Hours-level RTO and RPO is exactly the backup-and-restore profile: nothing runs in the second Region, only replicated snapshots and templates, which is the cheapest of the four strategies.
distractors: This is warm standby; it beats the objectives by a wide margin and costs far more.
A running standby tier is warm standby spend for a workload that only needs backup and restore.
Active-active is the most expensive strategy and the workload is not on DynamoDB.

stem: An application in private subnets across three Availability Zones sends high volumes of outbound traffic to third-party APIs through a single NAT gateway in one AZ. A review lists two problems: an AZ outage would take away egress everywhere, and the bill shows cross-AZ data transfer for traffic reaching the gateway. Which change addresses BOTH problems?
options: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance on a larger instance type with enhanced networking
Deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and route each private subnet to the NAT gateway in its own AZ
Attach an internet gateway to each private subnet so the instances reach the APIs directly
Move the NAT gateway into a public subnet in a different Region and route the subnets to it
explanation: A NAT gateway is zonal. One per AZ, with each AZ's private route table pointing at its local gateway, means an AZ outage only affects that AZ and traffic never crosses a zone boundary to reach the gateway, so the cross-AZ transfer charge disappears too.
distractors: A single NAT instance is still one zonal point of failure and adds management overhead.
Internet gateways attach to the VPC, not to subnets, and would make the subnets public.
A NAT Gateway serves subnets in its own VPC; it cannot live in another Region.

stem: A two-tier application uses an Auto Scaling group with a minimum of one instance in a single subnet and a single-AZ RDS MySQL instance. It must survive the loss of an Availability Zone with no data loss and automatic recovery. Which two changes are required? (Choose TWO.)
options: Span the Auto Scaling group across at least two AZs with a minimum of two instances behind an ELB
Add an RDS read replica in a second AZ
Replace the RDS instance with an Aurora Global Database in a second Region
Enable RDS Multi-AZ so a synchronous standby in another AZ takes over automatically
Store application session state on the instances' local EBS volumes
explanation: AZ resilience is an in-Region problem: compute must exist in more than one AZ with enough minimum capacity, and the database needs a synchronous standby that fails over automatically. Multi-AZ provides that; a read replica does not.
distractors: Read replicas are asynchronous and do not fail over automatically; they solve read scaling, not availability.
A second Region addresses Region failure and exceeds the requirement at much higher cost.
Local session state ties users to instances and is lost when an instance or AZ fails.

stem: A payments API runs active-standby across two Regions behind Network Load Balancers. Many clients are embedded devices that cache DNS for hours and firewalls that allow-list fixed IP addresses. Regional failover must complete within seconds. Which routing approach meets these requirements?
options: Route 53 failover records with health checks and a 10-second TTL on the records
Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks and a 10-second TTL on the records
AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups in both Regions and health checks
CloudFront with an origin group pointing at both Regional NLBs and origin failover
explanation: Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs that never change and shifts traffic between Regions in the AWS network within seconds, so failover does not depend on clients honouring DNS TTLs.
distractors: Any DNS-based failover is defeated by clients that ignore TTLs, and the answering IPs change on failover, breaking allow-lists.
Latency routing is still DNS-based and has the same caching and changing-IP problems.
CloudFront is for HTTP content delivery, has no fixed IPs and is not a fit for a TCP API needing allow-listed addresses.

stem: A media company must keep a copy of every uploaded object in a second Region and needs a contractual guarantee that objects are replicated within 15 minutes. What should they configure?
options: S3 Same-Region Replication with a lifecycle transition that moves objects to the second Region
S3 Cross-Region Replication with versioning on both buckets and S3 Replication Time Control
S3 Cross-Region Replication with Transfer Acceleration enabled on the destination bucket
An EventBridge rule that invokes a Lambda function to copy each object on upload within 15 minutes
explanation: CRR requires versioning on source and destination; Replication Time Control adds the SLA-backed commitment to replicate most objects within 15 minutes, which plain CRR does not offer.
distractors: Lifecycle rules change storage class; they cannot move objects to another Region, and SRR stays in one Region.
Transfer Acceleration speeds up client uploads over long distances; it does not provide a replication SLA.
A custom copier works but has no SLA and is more to build and operate than the native feature.

stem: An e-commerce checkout calls a third-party fulfilment API synchronously. When that API is slow or down, checkouts fail and orders are lost. The company wants orders to be accepted even when the fulfilment API is unavailable, with the LEAST change to the overall architecture. What should they do?
options: Increase the HTTP timeout and retry the fulfilment call up to ten times in the checkout request path
Deploy the checkout service in a second Region behind Route 53 failover records with health checks
Cache fulfilment responses in ElastiCache and serve the cached responses while the API is down
Write accepted orders to an SQS queue and have a separate consumer call the API with retries
explanation: Loose coupling turns a downstream outage into a backlog rather than an error: the checkout succeeds once the order is durably queued, and the consumer drains the queue when the API recovers.
distractors: Longer synchronous retries still block the checkout and fail once the API is down long enough.
The failure is in an external dependency, not in a Region; a second Region calls the same broken API.
Fulfilment requests are writes; caching prior responses does not create new fulfilment orders.

stem: A company has built a Multi-AZ architecture and written a failover runbook, but has never observed a real failure. Compliance now requires them to demonstrate quarterly that the system tolerates the loss of an AZ, using controlled, repeatable experiments with the LEAST custom tooling. Which service should they use?
options: AWS Fault Injection Service to run experiments that disrupt instances and network in one AZ
AWS Config rules that check every resource is deployed across at least two Availability Zones
CloudWatch Synthetics canaries that continuously probe the application endpoint from each AZ
AWS Resilience Hub assessments run against the CloudFormation stack before each quarterly review
explanation: Fault Injection Service runs managed chaos-engineering experiments, including AZ-disruption scenarios, so the runbook is exercised against real injected failure rather than assumed.
distractors: Config verifies configuration; it does not prove the system behaves correctly when an AZ actually fails.
Canaries detect outages; they do not cause the failure that the exercise must demonstrate recovery from.
Resilience Hub assesses and recommends against RTO/RPO targets; the actual fault-injection experiments are run by FIS.

stem: A single-AZ RDS for SQL Server instance backs a line-of-business application. A new requirement states that the database must survive an instance or AZ failure with no manual intervention, that failover must be transparent to the application, and that no data committed before the failure may be lost. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Create a cross-Region read replica and update the DNS record manually during an outage
Convert the instance to Multi-AZ so RDS fails over to a synchronous standby behind the same endpoint
Add an in-Region read replica and promote it to a standalone instance when the primary fails, then repoint the application
Take hourly snapshots and restore to a new instance with the same name if the primary fails
explanation: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ, so every committed write exists on both before the commit is acknowledged, and failover keeps the same DNS endpoint without operator action. Asynchronous replicas and snapshots both risk losing committed data.
distractors: Manual DNS updates violate the no-manual-intervention requirement, and cross-Region replication is asynchronous, so committed writes can be lost.
Promoting a read replica is a manual step, gives it a new endpoint, and replication is asynchronous.
Restoring from snapshots is manual, slow, and loses up to an hour of committed data.

stem: Lambda functions attached to private subnets in a VPC write several terabytes a day to S3 buckets in the same Region. The functions reach S3 through a NAT gateway, and its data-processing charge is now the largest line on the bill. Which change reduces this cost the MOST?
options: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the buckets so uploads take the edge path
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance on a larger instance type
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and route the private subnets to it
Remove the VPC configuration from the functions so they use the public S3 endpoint
explanation: A gateway endpoint carries S3 traffic over the AWS network with no hourly or per-GB charge, so the writes bypass the NAT gateway entirely. It applies to anything in the routed subnets, including VPC-attached Lambda functions.
distractors: Transfer Acceleration is for long-distance client uploads and adds cost; the traffic would still traverse the NAT gateway.
A NAT instance replaces the per-GB charge with instance cost and management, and still moves all bytes through one box.
Removing the VPC attachment would work for S3 but breaks whatever the functions are in the VPC to reach, and the question asks for a change to how S3 is reached.

stem: A news site serves images and video files directly from an S3 bucket to a global audience. Data-transfer-out charges are now the largest line on the bill. Which change reduces this cost with the LEAST effort?
options: Put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket
Move the objects to S3 One Zone-IA
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
Replicate the bucket to every Region where readers live
explanation: CloudFront serves repeat requests from edge caches, offloading the origin, and CloudFront egress pricing is lower than direct S3 egress to the internet.
distractors: Storage class changes storage cost, not data-transfer-out cost.
Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads and adds a per-GB charge; it does not reduce egress spend.
Multiple replicas add storage and replication cost while egress to the internet from each Region is still charged.

stem: A fleet of EC2 database servers uses 1 TB gp2 volumes that were sized that large only to obtain 3,000 IOPS; each holds about 200 GB of data. Which change reduces cost with NO loss of performance?
options: Convert the volumes to io2 and keep the current size to guarantee the IOPS
Convert the volumes to st1 throughput-optimised HDD and keep the current size
Snapshot the volumes and archive the snapshots to reduce the active storage charge
Migrate to gp3 volumes sized for the actual data and set IOPS independently
explanation: gp3 decouples IOPS from capacity and includes a 3,000 IOPS baseline at roughly 20% lower cost per GB than gp2, so the volumes can shrink to their real data footprint without losing performance.
distractors: io2 is a premium provisioned-IOPS volume that costs more, not less.
st1 is throughput-optimised HDD and cannot deliver 3,000 random IOPS for a database.
Snapshots do not reduce the size or cost of the live volumes.

stem: A DynamoDB table backing a ticketing system runs in on-demand capacity mode. Traffic follows a predictable daily pattern with a steady baseline and a lunchtime peak, and the table has become one of the largest cost items. Which change is the MOST cost-effective while still absorbing the peak?
options: Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to reduce the number of read requests billed
Switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling for reads and writes
Switch to provisioned capacity with fixed units sized for the lunchtime peak
Enable global tables so that traffic is spread over two Regions and billed lower
explanation: For predictable traffic, provisioned capacity is much cheaper per request than on-demand, and auto scaling adjusts the provisioned units through the daily peak so you do not pay for peak capacity all day.
distractors: DAX adds a paid cluster and only helps read-heavy workloads; it does not address the pricing mode.
Sizing fixed capacity for the peak pays for peak throughput 24 hours a day.
Global tables replicate writes to another Region and roughly double cost; they do not lower it.

stem: Analysts query two years of application logs stored in S3 as gzip-compressed JSON using Amazon Athena. Most queries filter by a single day and read three of forty fields, yet every query scans the whole data set and costs are high. What should be done to reduce Athena cost the MOST?
options: Convert the logs to Parquet, partition them by date, and update the Glue table
Move the logs to S3 Intelligent-Tiering so that rarely queried days are cheaper to scan
Provision a Redshift cluster, load the logs into it, and point the analysts at it
Increase the Athena workgroup's per-query data-scanned limit so queries finish
explanation: Athena bills per byte scanned. Columnar Parquet reads only the requested columns and date partitions restrict the scan to the relevant days, typically cutting scanned bytes by 90% or more.
distractors: Storage class changes storage cost; Athena still scans every byte of every query.
A cluster adds an always-on cost and does not answer the question of reducing Athena spend.
A scan limit caps individual queries; it does not reduce how much each query scans.

stem: A company runs a steady 24/7 web tier on EC2 that it plans to migrate to Fargate within the next year, and a nightly batch job that can be interrupted and restarted at any point. They want the LOWEST compute cost over the next three years. Which two purchasing choices should they make? (Choose TWO.)
options: Standard Reserved Instances for the web tier's current instance type
A Compute Savings Plan covering the web tier's baseline
On-Demand instances for the batch job so it always completes
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the batch job's instance family
Spot Instances for the batch job
explanation: A Compute Savings Plan discounts EC2 of any family and Region and carries over to Fargate and Lambda, so the planned migration does not strand the commitment. Interruptible batch is the textbook Spot workload at up to 90% off with no commitment.
distractors: Standard RIs are tied to a specific configuration and would be wasted when the tier moves to Fargate.
On-Demand is the most expensive way to run work that tolerates interruption.
Committing to a family for an interruptible job pays for capacity Spot would give far cheaper.

stem: A company will run a licensed database on a specific EC2 instance type in one Availability Zone for the next three years and must be guaranteed capacity in that AZ. There is a small chance the project is cancelled after 18 months, in which case they want to recoup part of the commitment. Which purchase option fits?
options: A three-year Compute Savings Plan for the instance
A three-year Convertible Reserved Instance for the instance type
A zonal Standard Reserved Instance for that instance type
A three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the family
explanation: Only Reserved Instances scoped to a zone reserve capacity, and only Standard RIs can be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace if plans change. Savings Plans reserve no capacity and cannot be sold.
distractors: Savings Plans are billing discounts only; they do not reserve capacity and cannot be resold.
Convertible RIs can be exchanged but cannot be sold on the Marketplace.
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is Regional, reserves no capacity and is not sellable.

stem: A company's monthly spend varies widely with customer activity, so fixed budget thresholds either fire constantly or never. They want to be told when spend on any service deviates from its normal pattern, without maintaining thresholds. Which tool should they use?
options: AWS Budgets with a monthly cost budget and a forecast alert
AWS Cost Explorer forecasts reviewed weekly by the finance team
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimisation checks with weekly emails
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with an alert subscription
explanation: Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn each service's normal spend and alerts on deviations, so no static thresholds are needed.
distractors: Budgets alerts on thresholds you set, which the scenario says are unworkable here.
Cost Explorer explains and forecasts spend but does not alert automatically on unusual behaviour.
Trusted Advisor finds idle or under-used resources; it does not watch spend patterns for anomalies.

stem: A FinOps team needs every billing line item, at hourly granularity with resource IDs and tags, so they can build custom chargeback dashboards with Athena and QuickSight. Which source should they use?
options: The Cost and Usage Report delivered to an S3 bucket
AWS Cost Explorer's grouped-by-tag view exported to CSV
AWS Budgets reports emailed monthly to the FinOps team
AWS Billing Conductor with a billing group per team
explanation: The CUR is the most detailed billing data set AWS provides, delivered as files to S3 and designed to be queried with Athena and visualised in QuickSight.
distractors: Cost Explorer is a console visualisation tool with limited granularity and is not a raw data feed for external dashboards.
Budgets reports summarise budget status; they are not line-item data.
Billing Conductor applies custom rates for internal showback; the underlying detail still comes from the CUR.

stem: A company notices its CloudWatch Logs storage bill grows every month even though the application's log volume is flat. Logs older than 90 days are only needed for occasional compliance queries. What is the MOST cost-effective fix?
options: Increase the log group's retention to 10 years so that older events are stored at a lower-cost tier
Set the log group retention to 90 days and export older logs to S3 with a lifecycle rule to Glacier
Enable CloudWatch Logs Insights on the log group so that stored log data is compressed
Stream all logs to Kinesis Data Streams with 90-day retention and delete the CloudWatch log groups
explanation: CloudWatch Logs keeps data forever by default, so ungrouped storage grows without limit. A retention setting bounds it, and exporting to S3 with a Glacier lifecycle keeps the rarely queried data at a fraction of the price.
distractors: Retention is already effectively unlimited; setting a long value does not reduce storage.
Logs Insights is a query engine; it does not change how much data is stored or billed.
Kinesis Data Streams is a transport with its own hourly cost, not a cheap archive.

stem: A company is migrating a Linux application to AWS. Multiple EC2 instances must read and write the same set of files concurrently through standard POSIX file operations. The team is offered a solution that rewrites the file layer to use S3 and one that mounts a shared network file system. The requirement is to migrate with MINIMAL changes to the application. Which solution should they choose?
options: Rewrite the file access layer to use the S3 API and store the files as objects in a single bucket
Mount an Amazon EFS file system on every instance and keep the file access code unchanged
Attach one EBS volume to all of the instances using Multi-Attach and a standard file system
Store the files in DynamoDB with S3 for large payloads and rewrite the file access layer
explanation: The qualifier is minimal application change. EFS presents a POSIX file system that the existing code can use as-is; the S3 rewrite would work but violates the qualifier.
distractors: Technically viable and often cheaper, but it requires rewriting the file layer, which the qualifier rules out.
Multi-Attach only works with io1/io2 volumes inside a single AZ and requires a cluster-aware file system; it does not give general shared POSIX access.
This is a full data-model rewrite and the opposite of minimal change.

stem: A genomics company runs a nightly analysis over the day's samples. The job takes about four hours on a fleet of EC2 instances, is checkpointed to S3 every few minutes, and can be restarted at any point; results are only needed by the next morning. Two designs are proposed: an On-Demand Auto Scaling group started on a schedule, and an AWS Batch compute environment using Spot Instances. Which should be chosen if the requirement is the MOST cost-effective solution?
options: The On-Demand Auto Scaling group, because it guarantees that the job completes before morning
Standard Reserved Instances sized for the fleet, because the job runs every night of the year
A single very large On-Demand instance started on a nightly schedule, because it finishes the job faster
The AWS Batch compute environment on Spot Instances, because the job is checkpointed and restartable
explanation: Both designs complete the job overnight, so the qualifier decides. A checkpointed, restartable, deadline-tolerant job is exactly the profile Spot is meant for, at up to 90% below On-Demand.
distractors: It works, but On-Demand pays full price for a workload that tolerates interruption; the qualifier is cost.
RIs charge for 24 hours a day of capacity to run a four-hour nightly job.
One large On-Demand instance is neither cheaper nor more resilient than a Spot fleet.

stem: An application on EC2 in a private subnet must read objects from an S3 bucket in the same Region. All four proposed designs let the application read the objects. Which is the MOST secure?
options: An IAM role on the instance profile with s3:GetObject on the bucket, and a gateway endpoint enforced by the bucket policy
An IAM user's access keys passed to the instance through user data, and a NAT gateway with a bucket policy allowing its Elastic IP
An IAM role on the instance profile with s3:* on all resources, and a NAT gateway with a bucket policy allowing the VPC CIDR
A public bucket policy allowing GetObject from the NAT gateway's Elastic IP, with an IAM role that has no S3 permissions
explanation: The most secure design combines least privilege (a role with only the needed action on the needed bucket), no long-lived credentials, and traffic that never leaves the AWS network, enforced by the bucket policy.
distractors: Long-lived access keys in user data are an anti-pattern that disqualifies the option outright.
The role is right but s3:* on all resources violates least privilege, and the traffic goes out through the internet path.
A public bucket relying on an IP allow-list is exposed to anyone sharing that egress IP and violates the no-public-access principle.

stem: A website emits clickstream events that must land in S3 as Parquet within a few minutes for downstream analytics. Two designs are offered: Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer that batches and writes files, and Kinesis Data Firehose with format conversion writing directly to S3. Which should be chosen if the requirement is NEAR real-time delivery with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Kinesis Data Streams with a Lambda consumer, because Streams offers sub-second latency
Kinesis Data Streams with an EC2 consumer using the Kinesis Client Library
Kinesis Data Firehose with Parquet format conversion delivering to S3
An SQS queue drained by an Auto Scaling group that writes Parquet files
explanation: The word "near" removes the need for sub-second delivery, and "least operational overhead" favours the fully managed delivery service. Firehose buffers, converts to Parquet and writes to S3 with no consumer code to run.
distractors: It works, but you now own consumer code, batching and file writing; the qualifier does not reward sub-second latency.
A KCL consumer on EC2 is the most operations-heavy option offered.
SQS plus a custom fleet requires the most code and infrastructure and offers no format conversion.

stem: A manufacturer needs a private, consistent low-latency link from its data centre to a VPC for daily operations, and the link must remain available if the primary connection fails. Two designs meet the requirement: two Direct Connect connections at separate locations, or one Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN as backup. Which should be chosen if the requirement is the MOST cost-effective highly available solution?
options: Two Direct Connect connections at separate locations, because both paths keep consistent latency
Two Site-to-Site VPN connections over the internet
One Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path
One Direct Connect connection with no backup, relying on the provider's SLA
